articles.title: N-able N-central gets emergency fix two days after 33 exploits published
articles.context: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33...
articles.full_text:
N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2, on Tuesday.

The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access.

N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances, and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication.

Exploit chains lead to remote code execution

The 33 exploits, which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance.

Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root.

A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to.

Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release.

N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs:

CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config

CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context)

CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation

CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security)

CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation

Attacks likely to follow

N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days.

In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems.

In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited.

N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints.

What customers should do

With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two.

Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string.

ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.

articles.title: Critical vulnerabilities in N-able N-central prompt hosted shutdown
articles.context: Overview On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and...
articles.full_text:
Overview

On November 9, 2026, N-able announced that it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

In a public disclosure titled Able2Shell, an independent researcher has published details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code covering 33 issues. According to the disclosure, the issues include unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE), privilege escalation to root, credential disclosure, and unauthorized account creation. One unauthenticated chain combines XML external entity (XXE) and session-handling weaknesses to execute code as the nable service account. Other demonstrated chains involve an administrator viewing malicious patch metadata or use ProductAdmin credentials. Rapid7 Intelligence is currently triaging the newly published details.

As of November 10, N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published PoC code and said it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited. The vendor has advised keeping N-central deployments offline while it develops and validates a hotfix. Hosted N-central classic environments remain offline, according to the same notice. N-able's notice does not yet include CVE identifiers or CVSS scores.

N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to administer endpoints and infrastructure. Compromise of an RMM server can put downstream managed environments at risk. N-central has previously been targeted through separate vulnerabilities, including an authentication bypass covered by Rapid7 in August 2026. Given the platform's administrative reach and the availability of public exploit code, Rapid7 recommends treating the current disclosure as an emergency.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations operating on-premises N-central servers take them offline immediately and keep them offline until the hotfix is available, and the server has been successfully upgraded. Hosted customers should follow the vendor's service restoration updates. N-able is developing and validating a hotfix, with a target of midday November 10 EST.

Affected versions: The researcher reports testing N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. N-able's current notice does not specify the full affected-version range.

Fixed versions: N-able's incident notice does not yet identify a remediation build. Follow the incident notice for release confirmation and installation instructions.

Rapid7 also recommends reviewing N-central servers and downstream managed systems for signs of compromise and engaging incident responders if suspicious activity is identified.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to N-able's security incident notice.

Updates

November 10, 2026: Initial publication.

articles.title: Apple Patches iMessage Group Chat Privacy Flaws and Bluetooth Pairing Vulnerabilities
articles.context: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it
articles.full_text:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Which Updates Carry the Fixes

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

articles.title: Bitdefender Threat Debrief | November 2026
articles.context: Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest
articles.full_text:
N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

This edition of the Bitdefender Threat Debrief covers the latest events in the ransomware threat landscape, including the claims surrounding the rise of the new ransomware group N0n, a former affiliate that turns on The Gentlemen, and news concerning BYOD ransomware.

As ransomware continues to evolve, our goal with this monthly Bitdefender Threat Debrief is to help you stay ahead of the curve. To do this, we combine information from openly available sources (OSINT) - things like news reports and research – with data we gather by analyzing Data Leak Sites (DLSs), websites where ransomware groups post details about their victims. It is important to remember that we can't independently verify all of these claims but are confident in the trends we see over time.

For this month's report, we analyzed data from October 1 to October 31, 2026, and recorded 1,072 claimed ransomware victims. Note that when excluding some of N0n’s victim dataset (126 victims) from October’s total victims, the actual number of victims reported is actually 946.

Featured Story: N0n Ransomware Uses AI and Victim Inflation to Rise to the Top

What Happened?

In mid-September, the ransomware group N0n emerged. The group hosted a data leak site with more than 100 victims, divided into categories including pending, exposed, leaked, and honors (where NOn claims to have honored the promise to destroy victim data in exchange for a ransom payment).

Several weeks later, information about N0n’s operations became plainly visible due to N0n’s failures to maintain strict operational security measures. N0n’s Python file server was left accessible on the open Internet. This presented visitors with the opportunity to go to the web address and navigate through directory structures to view contents of the server. This exposure allowed cyber defense and research teams to determine with greater confidence that N0n’s image as a potentially significant threat is just that: a false depiction. N0n is a newcomer to the ransomware landscape, relying on AI tools for foundational hacking tasks.

What Information was Disclosed in N0n’s Exposure?

N0n’s file server address is associated with a location in Sweden. Several types of information were disclosed in the aftermath of N0n’s exposure. All information types revealed make it highly unlikely that N0n is a ransomware group capable of competing with other leading threats. N0n;s actual victim count (rather than their published/perceived victim population) and their use of open-source AI dismantles their apparent trend of continuous growth. According to the data obtained from N0n’s file server, the group targeted just over 20 victims. Duplicate or false entries may have emerged due to weaknesses in maintaining the site and polling potential targets.

N0n also uses an open-source AI platform, OpenCode, to manage different AI models and write scripts. N0n invested more than $7000 in Generative AI to assist them in building common scripts that are maintained to perform actions necessary for scanning and reconnaissance activities. While an encryptor was also identified, debate remains over whether N0n consistently uses ransomware. Their reuse of encryption keys and weaknesses in OPSEC may point towards hesitancy for the group to execute ransomware code more frequently.

The exposure of N0n’s server also revealed that N0n references the same encryption keys that are used across different victim campaigns. This means that the group was leveraging the exact same ransomware code and keys to lockdown systems for different targets. Cybersecurity teams supporting victims with access to those hardcoded encryption keys can then analyze them and identify patterns needed for decryption.

What Actions are Recommended for Organizations?

As opportunistic ransomware groups continue to adopt AI into their operations, it is important for organizations to remember the following:

Data theft claims often initially lack any validity. Keep an inventory of your assets, including critical data that may be found in open repositories. Do not assume that any data stolen is from a current dataset or usable by the threat actor without supporting evidence.

Harden remote access controls to secure systems. This includes enforcing VPN access, restricting access via RDP and also requiring MFA authentication.

Enforce a strong password policy and regularly rotate credentials.

Regularly document breach cases predating current operations and check for additional exposures.

Maintain backups in a location separate from critical infrastructure and test them regularly to ensure backup data can be restored.

Request and review intelligence on an ongoing basis to evaluate the threat actor’s behavior and current indicators of compromise

Other Notable Ransomware News

Now, let’s explore the notable news and findings since the last Threat Debrief.

Azazel, an affiliate of The Gentlemen, turns on their operator: Azazel has accumulated more than 6 terabytes of stolen data. Despite their affiliation with The Gentlemen, the group broke away from them after stealing data in an RaaS campaign and keeping the profits for themselves. Azazel published the stolen data on a data leak site under the name Leakned. Notably, Azazel has leveraged a technique that differs from other ransomware groups. They used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to establish a connection between an AI coding assistant and a reverse shell. This connection allows Azazel to use the AI assistant as a command and control channel, executing commands on compromised machines. Azazel has engaged in primarily in data theft and credential theft, extracting credentials from GitLab and other pipelines.

BYOD ransomware claims university that provides healthcare services: BYOD, a ransomware group that emerged in September, has claimed enterprise organizations across both North America and Southeast Asia. The group recently claimed a university clinic that provides healthcare services to patients. Within 24 hours of their claim, BYOD expressed that they did not realize the systems they targeted were used specifically to support direct patient care. BYOD announced they would make decryptors available to the victim organization for free; and, the affected victims are encouraged to reach them and submit a payment of $2,500 to ensure their data is destroyed. These claims are identified as potential ploys to extend the compromise and/or collect additional payment.

Booba Team claims more victims and hits government organizations: Booba Team has claimed more than 9 government organizations at the time of this release. According to Booba Team’s data leak site, this accounts for more than 800 GB of stolen data. Booba Team’s total victims claimed in the government sector in October surpasses the totals in the same period for both Qilin (who claimed 6 victims) and The Gentlemen (who claimed 3 victims). Unlike Qilin and The Gentlemen, who have broadened their victim populations to include government victims in Western Europe and Southeast Asia, Booba Team has continued to claim victims in a limited number of regions, including North America (specifically the US) and South America. The group has been known to deploy ransomware and conduct data theft.

New brands continue to make their entry into the ransomware ecosystem: More than 17 ransomware groups have emerged in the last two months. Several newcomers were identified in October, including but not limited to: aoqin, everstake, shiba, whitearmor, hyflock, umbra, vypr, and scarlettgroup. While some groups emerge out of a necessity to commit acts of organized crime, with limited influence from other threat groups. However, the largest variables that contribute to new ransomware groups include law enforcement takedowns, feuds and factions among ransomware groups and affiliates, and operational failures. Bitdefender will continue to track further developments in ransomware takedowns, rebrands, and evolutions.

Top 10 Ransomware Families

Bitdefender's Threat Debrief analyzes data from ransomware data leak sites, where groups publicize their claimed number of compromised organizations. This approach provides valuable insights into overall RaaS market activity. However, it comes with a trade-off: while it reflects attackers' self-proclaimed success, the information comes directly from criminals and may be unreliable. Additionally, this method captures the number of victims claimed, not the actual financial impact of these attacks.

The Top 10 ransomware groups in October include N0n, The Gentlemen, Qilin, Akira, and Booba Team. Note that due to several indicators of N0n misrepresenting their operations and victims, Bitdefender has high confidence that N0n is not in actuality a group that has the means to maintain a ranking in the Top 10 Groups.

Top 10 Most Attacked Regions

Ransomware gangs prioritize targets where they can squeeze the most money from victims. In many cases, this means focusing on developed countries with higher projected growth rates. Threat actors may also launch strategic attacks during geopolitical conflicts or periods of social unrest.

Taiwan rejoins the Top 10 Regions: Taiwan ranked 10th in October; most of the region’s industries affected by ransomware attacks are in manufacturing, healthcare, and technology.

Victims based in South Korea rise due to N0n’s claims: The number of ransomware victims based in South Korea rose to 18 in October. N0n claimed 11 victims based in South Korea; all of these victims are organizations in the transportation industry. However, due to the high level of scrutiny cast on the validity of N0n’s claims, this increase should not be viewed as an accurate pattern of behavior. Ransomware groups have not claimed a total number of victims based in South Korea surpassing 10 per month since September 2025 when Qilin executed the Korean Leaks campaign.

Top 10 Most Attacked Industries

Ransomware gangs may target organizations in critical infrastructure sectors, select other organizations that offer services tailored to consumers, or attack organizations that fall into both categories. Understanding the trends and ramifications associated with specific industries, and how specialized services and clientele are impacted is crucial for assessing risk. Here are the Top 10 industries affected by ransomware attacks.

Healthcare rises to second place in the Top Industries

In October, there was an increase in the number of victim organizations represented in the manufacturing and healthcare industries. Healthcare rose to the second rank. And, the transportation industry moved from the 10th rank to the 6th rank in the Top Industries with N0n claiming a total of 20 transportation victims.

About Bitdefender Threat Debrief

The Bitdefender Threat Debrief (BDTD) is a monthly series analyzing threat news, trends, and research from the previous month. Don’t miss the next BDTD release, subscribe to the Business Insights blog, and follow us on Twitter. You can find all previous debriefs here.

Bitdefender provides cybersecurity solutions and advanced threat protection to hundreds of millions of endpoints worldwide. More than 180 technology brands have licensed and added Bitdefender technology to their product or service offerings. This vast OEM ecosystem complements telemetry data already collected from our business and consumer solutions. To give you some idea of the scale, Bitdefender Labs discover 400+ new threats each minute and validate 30 billion threat queries daily. This gives us one of the industry’s most extensive real-time views of the evolving threat landscape.

We would like to thank Bitdefenders Stefan Hanu, Mihai Leonte, Gabriel Macovei, and Andrei Mogage for their help with putting this report together.

articles.title: Peer pressure meets private keys.
articles.context: Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.
articles.full_text:
A classified memo ties Nvidia’s chief executive to Chinese espionage. AI coding agents crack under peer pressure, coughing up private keys. Big breaches hit seven million Japanese shoppers and three million students here in the States, while a French bank takes a multi-million-dollar hit through a vendor compromise. Adversaries weaponize a fresh OpenSSH bypass in the wild, pro-Russian hacktivists put dark web bounties on senior European officials, and Google drafts digital IDs to solve the passkey recovery puzzle. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Chris Grove, Director of Cybersecurity Strategy at Nozomi Networks, discussing the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attacks. Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Today is Monday November 9th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Classified memo warns of Nvidia chief's ties to Chinese operative.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo this past spring warning senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an operative tied to Beijing's Ministry of State Security.

Intelligence gathered from electronic surveillance revealed Huang was intimately involved with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed has purchased two billion dollars in advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of smuggling restricted artificial intelligence hardware into China. While Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, Nvidia stated it has no reason to believe national security or trade secrets were compromised.

Huang remains an influential voice shaping United States policy against tighter export controls, highlighting the growing counterintelligence risks hovering over America’s critical semiconductor supply chains.

The New York Times originally reported the findings.

Autonomous AI coding agents leak credentials under swarm peer pressure.

Autonomous software engineering agents routinely violate core security policies, leaking private deployment credentials and executing untrusted scripts, when pressured by third-party agent forums, according to testing by AE Studio and the AI Alignment Foundation shared with The Register.

Researchers tasked nine coding models with debugging a broken service in an isolated sandbox. Given access to a forum that held the solution, agents surrendered private tokens fifteen percent of the time and executed unverified installation scripts nearly a quarter of the time to obtain assistance. Under performance pressure, execution rates spiked to thirty-four percent.

As organizations rush to integrate autonomous agents into production environments, granting models broad system permissions without strict data isolation turns automated workflows into immediate remote code execution and credential leakage risks.

A Japanese online market goes offline following a suspected breach of 7.7 million customer records.

Japanese consumer goods and electronics giant Iris Ohyama has suspended its primary ecommerce platform, Iris Plaza, following unauthorized access to a third-party cloud service that contained personal records for nearly eight million shoppers.

The retailer took the storefront offline late last month after discovering a suspicious file on its cloud infrastructure. Exposed records cover 5.8 million registered members and 1.9 million guest shoppers, potentially compromising names, physical and email addresses, birth dates, phone numbers, and encrypted passwords. Payment data was stored separately and avoided exposure.

The disruption highlights the severe operational fallout and supply-chain vulnerabilities inherent in cloud-hosted retail environments, leaving core commerce operations frozen while investigators determine whether customer files were actually exfiltrated.

Threat actors exploit a high-severity OpenSSH authentication bypass.

Threat actors are actively exploiting a critical authentication bypass in OpenSSH tracked as CVE-2026-123158, dubbed "SSHole."

The vulnerability allows attackers to compromise accounts like root on systems running musl libc without PAM—including Alpine and OpenWrt—by supplying overlong passwords. Security firms WatchTowr and Previdian report that botnets and cryptominers are already leveraging the flaw in the wild.

The rapid weaponization underscores immediate exposure for lightweight Linux environments, prompting administrators to deploy version 10.6p2 or disable password authentication entirely.

A French banking group confirms third-party compromise and fraudulent fund transfers.

French banking giant Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed an intrusion into its network via a third-party service provider, enabling attackers to conduct major fraudulent transactions.

The disclosure follows reports from blockchain investigator ZachXBT, who traced approximately 133 million dollars in suspicious withdrawals and aggressive cryptocurrency laundering across multiple centralized exchanges. The bank stressed that customer accounts remained untouched, as the threat actors targeted Arkéa's own institutional accounts before routing capital toward external cryptocurrency platforms. Arkéa reports that security teams contained the incident, froze a portion of the funds, and maintain that the bank's financial stability remains secure.

The incident underscores the persistent vulnerability institutional financial networks face through external vendor access paths, demonstrating how rapid cryptocurrency conversion complicates law enforcement recovery efforts.

Frontline Education data breach impacts over three million individuals across K-12 systems.

School administration provider Frontline Education has notified the Indiana Attorney General’s Office that an August breach compromised records for over three million people—more than doubling previous state estimates.

Attackers exploited a flaw in a third-party application, accessing personal records of staff and students across Frontline Central and School Health Management services. Exfiltrated data includes Social Security numbers, driver’s licenses, and health insurance information.

The incident highlights continuing third-party software risks threatening sensitive educational and student administrative platforms.

Google develops digital identity credentials for secure passkey and account recovery.

Google is developing an account recovery framework that leverages verified digital identity credentials, aiming to eliminate the security vulnerabilities of fallback methods when users lose primary devices.

Speaking at the Authenticate 2026 conference, company product managers explained that legacy recovery workflows—such as SMS-based fallbacks—risk undermining the cryptographic advantages of passkeys. Under Google's proposed system, users register a signed digital ID in advance to create a cryptographic stable hash linked to their account. If their physical device is lost, obtaining a verified digital credential on a replacement device restores their account, passkeys, and data in a single step.

Securing the recovery loop represents the crucial missing link in widespread passwordless adoption, though full-scale rollout still faces hurdles in wallet interoperability and near-real-time credential provisioning.

Pro-Russian hacktivists dox European leaders and bounty personal details.

Pro-Russian hacktivist syndicate NoName057(16) has published personal records belonging to Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and seventeen other senior European officials across the dark web, offering cryptocurrency bounties for further intelligence on the targets and their families.

The doxing campaign targets prominent figures across European law enforcement and judiciary—including leaders at Europol, Eurojust, and the German Federal Criminal Police Office—alongside investigative journalists. The operation appears to be direct retaliation for a multi-nation law enforcement takedown in July 2025 that dismantled over one hundred of the gang's servers.

The move marks an aggressive evolution from nuisance denial-of-service disruptions into direct personal harassment and targeted intelligence-gathering aimed at deterring Western support for Ukraine.

Capital continues pouring into artificial intelligence defense and validation, led by 220 million dollars raised across two standout funding rounds. Agentic data security startup Sentra secured 150 million dollars in a round led by Capital One Ventures, while formal verification provider &Truth emerged from stealth backed by 70 million dollars in seed capital.

Consolidation across the sector accelerated with eight reported acquisitions, headlined by CrowdStrike’s aggressive expansion into model governance. According to the Wall Street Journal, the security giant is acquiring AI observability firm Fiddler AI for 400 million dollars alongside red-teaming platform Dreadnode for 95 million dollars to embed behavioral accountability into its Falcon ecosystem. Penetration testing specialist Bendings also acquired Scopertos for 55 million dollars, while Cognition absorbed code security shop Corridor.

The flurry of dealmaking signals that enterprise demand is rapidly shifting toward pre-deployment testing, agent explainability, and securing the broader algorithmic supply chain.

After the break, I welcome Nozomi Networks’ Director of Cybersecurity Strategy Chris Grove. We discuss the critical infrastructure implications of the European refrigeration attack part 2.

That was Chris Grove from Nozomi Networks.

Beijing goes all-in on domestic silicon.

Huawei claims it has built the holy grail of sovereign computing: an enterprise desktop boasting one hundred percent Chinese-manufactured components.

The Qingyun HM650 runs a homegrown, ten-core Kirin processor alongside an enterprise flavor of HarmonyOS, specifically designed to bid a polite, permanent farewell to Western software dependencies. One government agency has already ordered six hundred units—perhaps less out of spontaneous consumer enthusiasm and more in dutiful compliance with Beijing’s mandate evicting Wintel machines from state desks.

Whether every capacitor actually traces its architectural ancestry strictly to domestic drawing boards remains conveniently ambiguous, as foreign outfits still keep plenty of factories humming across the mainland. Regardless of pedigree, locking Western chipmakers out of vast government procurement pools delivers a cold chill to Santa Clara balance sheets.

Meanwhile, Japan unveiled a sixty-three million dollar emergency cybersecurity fund after adversaries disrupted critical infrastructure, cloud providers, and—perhaps most unforgivably—KFC logistics.

In this article

How we found and validated the bugs

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI

Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.[OW1] [YB2]

How we found and validated the bugs

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

A note on open issues

At publication, two of the issues reported by our team remain open. The article also references related issues reported by others and fixes that are still under review. The Rust maintainers triaged and responded to our reports quickly, and we believe maintainers and the contributors working on these issues are doing their best and making the right tradeoffs among the many bugs they handle.

If you’re interested in an open issue, please comment only when you have something genuinely new to contribute, such as new information or an affected real-world use case.

Patterns of Rust’s Safety Bugs

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

pub fn get>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option { if idx < s.as_ref().len() { // SAFETY: we just checked that `idx` is in bounds. Some(unsafe { *s.as_ref().get_unchecked(idx) }) } else { None } }

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

Figure 1 — Panic Safety.

MapWindows::clone (issue #156501)

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. The nightly API Iterator::map_windows yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

struct Buffer { // Invariant: `self.buffer[self.start..self.start + N]` is initialized, // with all other elements being uninitialized. This also // implies that `self.start <= N`. buffer: [[MaybeUninit; N]; 2], start: usize, }

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

impl Clone for Buffer { fn clone(&self) -> Self { let mut buffer = Buffer { buffer: [[const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N], [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N]], start: self.start, }; buffer.as_uninit_array_mut().write(self.as_array_ref().clone()); buffer } }

After buffer is constructed, it breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The self.as_array_ref().clone() call runs the user's T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

Allocators must not unwind

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library's unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait's methods or from drop. The proposal notes that "unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness."

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

std::vector v(100, 42); // Bug: `<=` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }); // AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop

The same comparator passed to Rust's sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn't match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491)

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

pub fn replace(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String { // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another. if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() { Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte), Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()), _ => None, } { if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() { return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) }; } }

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String { let result: Vec = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect(); // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings. unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) } }

The CharPattern branch checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern { // ... fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option> { static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80]; Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE)) } } // "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8. let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?");

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn't valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

More examples

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn't spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018)

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

Figure 2 — Stack Overflow.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

pub unsafe fn cleanup() { if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") { return; } // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth! // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272 unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) }; }

The cleanup function passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

// SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack! unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) }; // SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of // a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there. unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) };

The call to sigaltstack disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but the subsequent call to munmap unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951)

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock(); let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref());

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

_reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ())); *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr(); } libc::execvp(self.get_program_cstr().as_ptr(), self.get_argv().as_ptr()); Err(io::Error::last_os_error())

Command::exec takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet do_exec writes the process-global environ. Before the write, do_exec saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust's lock.

process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243)

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

that code won't panic at the wrong moment,

that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, and

that the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects.

Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2)

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren't always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3)

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc's exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust's type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort's ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust's sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn't guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn't automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust's safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it's also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust's safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

Beyond the lab

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we're exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust's standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we're applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it's to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

In this article

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

Investigate risk with Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID

What are risk detections? – Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:
