articles.full_text:
The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.

Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.

With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.

Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.

This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.

But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.

What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE

Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.

One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.

One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.

Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.

However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.

This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.

An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.

Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.

A feast of cryptography

When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.

Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.

Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.

We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.

This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.

VOLE-in-the-Head

The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.

Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.

One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).

Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.

The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.

When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.

Multivariate signatures

Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.

The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.

UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures.

The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough.

Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOV

Earlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published (Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often.

This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions. But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail.

A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment. For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly.

To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof.

Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer:

The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer.

The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash.

Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1,

The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m.

Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions.

The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.)

Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) where s is the signature, rs is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting.

From blind signatures to endorsements and beyond

Recall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P1,…,PN, and the statement we now want to prove is Pi(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) for some anchor key Pi whose index i is now part of the hidden witness.

With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter.

Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH.

Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board.

Optimizations

Before we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions.

On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve.

Using fewer hashes

PoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.

This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.

This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.

In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.

Making each hash cheaper

Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.

Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.

Leaning into multivariate

In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.

This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.

We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.

Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).

For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.

There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.

And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.

Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?

We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.

Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:

issuance

presentation

PoMFRIT (with UOV)

<1KB

4.3KB (redemption)

VOLE-IHAT

5.6KB

6.5KB (redemption)

VOLE-ACT

5.4KB

12.0KB (spend)

These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)

If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.

We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

articles.full_text: India’s Computer Emergency Response Team has warned the nation’s financial services industry of a “significant escalation” in attacks by what it describes as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor” that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts. CERT-IN first detected the attacks in October and issued advisory in which it warned digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If the attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money. On Thursday, the CERT published an update in which it said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents. “The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response,” the CERT warned. CERT-IN has decided the attackers need a name and chose “CRAFTY FALCON.” The security org has also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX pen-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework – all of which have been linked to users who appear to speak Chinese. CRAFTY FALCON’s tactics see it go looking for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens, or network paths that help it move into production systems. If it gets in, the crew re-writes victims’ applications so they do things like make unauthorized API calls. Victims’ defenses assume that only legitimate apps would call those APIs, so activity conducted by the re-written apps aren’t flagged as an attack. Even if victims suspect an attack, they have a lot to cope with because CERT-IN says CRAFTY FALCON creates many “functionally identical variants refined in rapid succession; a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.” The crew also quickly exploits newly discovered vulnerabilities to keep its attacks fresh. Once it gets a toehold, the criminal crew makes tiny payments of about $0.01 to test if its attacks work. If those transfers work, CRAFTY FALCON makes larger payments. When the target is a cryptocurrency exchange or virtual digital asset service provider, the crew steals wallet keys and empties cryptocurrency wallets. Vendors of observability tools will be warming up their Indian sales teams today, because CERT-IN’s advice to Indian businesses includes improving their ability to log events, monitor for anomalies in real time, and send alerts. It also urged keeping test environments off the internet, and restricting access to cloud resources because CRAFTY FALCON is fond of using them to run its attacks. CERT-IN also warns that the attacks are “active and escalating” and therefore worthy of 24x7 monitoring. Interestingly, the CERT’s advisory mentions attacks on “entities” across banking, financial services, and insurance, but only names the kind of businesses mentioned above as having reported attacks. The Register points this out because India is home to literally thousands of banks, many of them small operations that sometimes lack basic infosec protections. CRAFTY FALCON therefore has a target-rich environment in India should it choose to expand its activities. ®

articles.title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
articles.context: Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks...
articles.full_text:
In this article

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Follow-on actions

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Microsoft detections

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization.

Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. A similar campaign involving the same IPs addressed was also reported by Todyl. Separately, Microsoft observed reconnaissance operations from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads deployed by victims on Azure AI services.

Microsoft encourages organizations to scan their code in GitHub and determine where any secrets are present. In addition to removing the secrets from the code base, affected organizations should immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. GitHub monitors public repositories by automatically scanning for secrets. In addition to scanning their own repositories, organizations can enable public monitoring through GitHub to detect secrets leaked in secondary public repositories across GitHub. This extends secret scanning beyond the repositories an enterprise owns to follow potential secret exposure across the platform. GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps scans for credentials and other sensitive content in source code. Push protection can also block supported secrets before they’re pushed. Organizations need either GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps or, for organizations using the standalone experience, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps enabled.

Secrets are exposed in public repositories when code containing the secret is committed to GitHub. Developers might store secrets in configuration files, scripts, or other code to quickly operationalize the OAuth application or avoid configuring more modern authentication flows. Organizations can reduce exposure by protecting workload identities and secrets, enforcing least privilege, safeguarding recovery resources, and enabling relevant Microsoft Defender for Cloud protections. Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure. Microsoft recommends that developers migrate OAuth applications away from secret-based authentication. While storing long-lived application client secrets in code is a common practice, using managed identities for application authentication eliminates the possibility of secret exposure in code, manual processes associated with secret management, and barriers to securely scaling applications.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Starting in August 2026, Microsoft observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to submit large volumes of queries to GitHub for secrets. The queries submitted by the AI framework often included the name of a target organization, keywords for secrets, a keyword linked to cloud services, or a keyword linked to another AI service provider. Organizations that find their secrets exposed in public repositories must assume that the exposed secrets and associated applications are compromised.

Follow-on actions

Credential abuse via Entra ID

In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, an agentic framework used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins primarily came from two IP addresses: 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. The latter IP address is a Tor exit node, which might be associated with unrelated malicious activity, including from unrelated sources. The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants.. Service principals are the identities that applications use to authenticate and give direct, programmatic access to whatever the application is authorized to reach.

The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access. In some tenants, the threat actor sent Microsoft Graph API requests, which were mostly searches to find content of interest. The threat actor enumerated subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments, and service configurations in Azure to map the environment.

Additionally, the threat actor attempted to validate stolen Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, as identified using Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection. Observed activity suggests that the threat actor might have attempted to abuse some of these compromised AI resources to facilitate their broader attack activity.

Figure 1. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain

Cloud API adjustments indicative of adaptive behavior

Additionally in this attack the agent’s operations on a victim’s Azure Resource Manager (ARM) instance originating from 199.19.77[.]84 demonstrated sequences consistent with adaptive troubleshooting, where failed cloud API requests were followed by changes to HTTP methods or API versions and subsequent HTTP 200 responses:

A batch of ARM requests attempting to enumerate secret metadata across multiple Azure Key Vault resources returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). These requests specified a version associated with Key Vault’s data-plane APIs against ARM (control-plane) APIs. Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200.

A GET request to enumerate an Azure SQL server’s firewall rules specified an outdated API version and returned HTTP 400. Approximately 60 seconds after that request, a matching GET began using a supported version and subsequently returned HTTP 200. The URL changed only in its api-version parameter.

An ARM POST request to an Application Insights query endpoint returned HTTP 400 because an outdated API version was specified. Approximately 80 seconds after the failed request, another POST began against the same endpoint, specifying a supported API version, and subsequently returned HTTP 200.

OAuth application abuse

In multiple cases, Microsoft observed the same agentic AI tools subsequently obtain a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In some cases, the agents exfiltrated secrets from the organization’s Azure Key Vault. The agents once authenticated have also searched Azure DevOps for secrets. Until the secrets are revoked or rotated, they can allow a threat actor to maintain persistence in the organization, compromise additional identities, or hijack resources. In one observed case, an AI agent progressed from searching for the client secrets in GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

The agents also used the compromised OAuth application to use the Run Command, which runs scripts in Azure VMs. With access to this functionality on a VM, a threat actor can access unsecured credentials and other stored data, compromise associated workload identities, or run code that provides persistence or lateral movement.

During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services). Multiple public reports have documented threat actors using agentic AI tools to compromise credentials for AI services, sometimes to run the same agentic AI workflow.

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Microsoft recommends the following mitigation steps to contain, detect, and investigate this threat.

Containment

Block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy targeting workload identities, assigned directly to service principals, and in a user-scoped block policy to cover replayed sessions. Note that workload identity policies require Workload ID Premium licensing and cover only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. Block the exact IP rather than the whole ASN.

For affected users, revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys.

For any affected application, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including those added by the threat actor and disable the service principal if needed. Tokens already issued remain valid until expiry.

Rotate everything stored in any Key Vault the affected application could read, and any credentials found in accessed documents.

MSPs: Review Partner Center access, GDAP relationships, and customer tenants, and notify affected customers per your agreements.

Detection and hunting

Review Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18 including failed attempts. Sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS7000222 (expired secret) indicate someone holds a credential for your app; a failure followed by a success is urgent.

Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and Microsoft 365 unified audit logs for the address, including secret reads, blob and file downloads, and changes to apps, permissions or pipelines.

In Azure DevOps auditing, review PAT creation and first use, federated service connections, pipeline runs and edits, and unfamiliar user agents. Enable auditing if it is off.

Look for behavior as well as the IP: one address authenticating to three or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. Search as far back as retention allows.

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Threat actors can and do change the source IP address, user agent strings, and other fingerprints left by the agentic AI penetration testing tools they use. This can make identifying and blocking malicious network traffic early difficult for defenders.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

Protect and continuously assess application credentials and secrets. Avoid storing service principal credentials, storage keys, connection strings, and other secrets in source code, configuration files, public repositories, issues, or other locations where they might be inadvertently exposed. To find credentials in source code, consider using tools like GitHub Advanced Security or other OWASP source code analysis tools.

Rotate compromised or exposed credentials immediately and establish credential lifecycle practices. Treat credentials that have been publicly exposed as compromised, even if the original location has subsequently been edited or deleted. Removing the content does not invalidate the credential or eliminate copies retained in edit history, caches, archives, logs, or other systems. Immediately revoke or rotate the affected credentials and investigate their historical use. Where supported, organizations should favor mechanisms that reduce reliance on long-lived credentials. Learn more about protecting secrets with Defender for Cloud.

Enable appropriate Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads. Consider enabling workload protections relevant to the resources in your environment, including Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for Storage, Defender for Key Vault, Defender for App Service, and Defender for Databases. Learn more in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview.

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities. Review the Azure role-based access control (RBAC) permissions assigned to service principals and restrict their privileges to the resources and operations required by their applications. Learn more about best practices for Azure RBAC.

Protect backup and recovery infrastructure as part of resilience. Restrict access to backup and recovery resources and closely monitor attempts to modify or remove their protection controls. Learn more about Azure Backup security best practices.

Hardening OAuth applications against compromise involves managing the permissions of the applications in your organization and securing application secrets. To triage applications in your environment, enforce security policies with new applications as they are created, and address existing applications over time beginning with the most recent ones.

Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The Cloud app catalog page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate.

Use Conditional Access policies for workload identities. Consider augmenting identity signals with workload identity risk protection.

Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the application developer role to privileged users. Review the list of least privileged roles by task to help scope role-based access control in your environment.

Integrate enterprise applications with Microsoft Entra ID.

Microsoft detections

Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

Tactic

Observed activity

Microsoft Defender and Sentinel coverage

Initial access

Multiple identity-protection alerts identified authentication attempts from anonymized or high-risk infrastructure. This pattern can indicate attempted access through proxy, VPN, or previously reported malicious network sources.

Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Anonymous IP address

Initial access

Attack-analysis detections identified OAuth application activity consistent with compromise. This type of detection is useful when evaluating whether an app identity, rather than only a user identity, may have been abused.

Microsoft Defender XDR – Potentially compromised OAuth application identified through attack activity analysis

Initial access, Discovery

Unattributed network indicators related to ARTEX use are flagged by Microsoft Threat Intelligence research and surfaced across multiple alerts. Suspected ARTEX use can include activity beyond the GitHub repository scanning activity discussed in this blog.

Microsoft Sentinel – Abnormal Deny Rate for Source IP– Abnormal Port to Protocol– Inbound Network Attack detected– Malformed user agent– Password spray attack against Azure AD application Microsoft Defender XDR – Account compromised following a password-spray attack– Anomalous OAuth device code authentication activity– Multiple Service Principal Sign-ins from Single IP– Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP addressMicrosoft Defender for Cloud Apps – Activities from suspicious user agents– Multiple failed login attempts– Multiple failed user log on attempts to an app– OAuth application activity from an uncommonly visited ISP– Suspicious OAuth app registration Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Key vault unusual access denied – user/application accessing high volume of denied key vaults– Access from an unusual location to a sensitive blob container– Azure Resource Manager operation from suspicious IP address Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Atypical travelMalicious IP addressPassword Spray– Verified threat actor IP

Credential access

Identity-protection detections observed password spray behavior. This indicates repeated authentication attempts across accounts or tenants using a common source pattern.

Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Password spray Microsoft Defender for Identity – Suspicious service principal sign-in following credential addition

Credential access

Azure Key Vault access

Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Defender for Key Vault) – Unusual operation pattern in a key vault– High volume of operations in a key vault– Unusual application accessed a key vault– Suspicious secret listing and query in a key vault– Unusual access to the key vault from a suspicious IP (Non-Microsoft or External)

Command and control

Suspicious Microsoft Graph API usage was observed from campaign infrastructure. The activity involved Graph requests that can support discovery, collection, or follow-on cloud operations.

Microsoft Defender for Identity– Suspicious Entra Graph API query observed

Advanced hunting queries

The following hunting queries are related to the October 28 Entra ID service principal sign-in activity.

Find successful and failed application sign-ins from the suspicious IP addresses

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, Application, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalName, ServicePrincipalId, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceId, ResourceTenantId, IPAddress, ErrorCode, UserAgent, CorrelationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc

Find Microsoft Graph API requests from the two IP addresses, including searches and response status

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); GraphAPIAuditEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IpAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalId, AccountObjectId, IpAddress, RequestMethod, RequestUri, ResponseStatusCode, ResponseSize, Scopes, EntityType, TargetWorkload, UniqueTokenIdentifier, ClientRequestId, OperationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc

Find available Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Azure cloud activity details from the suspicious IP addresses

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, Application, CloudAppId = ApplicationId, ActionType, ActivityType, AccountType, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, UserAgent, ObjectName, ObjectType, ObjectId, ActivityObjects, ReportId, RawEventData | order by Timestamp asc

CloudAuditEvents table to identify suspicious controlplane operations

CloudAuditEvents | where IPAddress has_any ('199.19.77.84','65.87.223.26')

CloudStorageEvents table to identify possible exfiltration from Storage Accounts.

CloudStorageAggregatedEvents | where IPAddress in ('199.19.77.84','65.87.223.26') | where SuccessfulOperationsCount > 0

Microsoft Security Copilot

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

Customers can also deploy AI agents, including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents, to perform security tasks efficiently:

Threat Intelligence Briefing agent

Phishing Triage agent

Threat Hunting agent

Dynamic Threat Detection agent

Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Activity Profile: Stolen application credentials used to sign in as Entra ID workload identities and access Azure, Microsoft 365 resources

Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat.

Learn more

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

articles.title: Introducing AWS account access manager: IAM role flexibility with centralized workforce access
articles.context: Account access manager launch partners Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into...
articles.full_text:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.

Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.

Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.

Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:

Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.

Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.

IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.

Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).

Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.

For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.

Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

Sign in to your organization’s management account.

In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.

The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.

If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \ --region <Region> \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": "<IAM Identity Center Instance ARN>" } }'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.

Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws

Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*

Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws

Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws

Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access

Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace <your-account-id>, <region> (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and <application-id> (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "<your-account-id>", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:<region>:<your-account-id>:application/<application-id>" } } } ] }

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/<key> and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.

Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.

Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.

Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region <Region> \ --application-arn "<Account_access_manager_ARN>" \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": "<Identity_Center_User_ID>" } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME>" } }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "<IDC_GROUP_ID>". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.

Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.

IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.

Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.

Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.

On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.

Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.

Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.

Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).

Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.

On the AWS CLI, run:

aws login

Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).

Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.

Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary

Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.

Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.

Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.

Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.

Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.

Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.

Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.

Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide. We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment.

Moumita is a Sr. Identity Specialist Solutions Architect, currently driving identity innovation, she builds customer solutions, shapes product direction, and advances access management practices across industries. With over 14 years of security expertise, she has delivered high-impact security innovations for Fortune 500 enterprises and Global Systems Integrator partners.

With 15 years of security experience spanning multiple industries, his goal is to help customers understand and improve their security and compliance posture in a scalable way. He tackles global security challenges through content creation, teaching, knowledge sharing, and contributing to global standards and organizational bodies.
