He works with large enterprises across industries like Media & Entertainment and Healthcare and Life Sciences to help secure their most critical workloads and find new ways to innovate securely. He is based out of Seattle with over 7 years of experience.

articles.title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
articles.context: Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed,...
articles.full_text:
On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration, and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now, which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security.

Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now.

Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation.

Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure.

This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default.

Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain.

Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default

Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads.

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. Building on protections available today, it progressively establishes and maintains more of the recommended security posture through the products themselves, adapting the baseline as threats and Microsoft security guidance evolve.

The result is less manual effort and a stronger security posture maintained increasingly through the products themselves. We’re advancing this work across three areas: Patch, Configure, and Protect.

Figure 1: On-Premises Baseline Security Mode builds on capabilities available today across Patch, Configure, and Protect, with greater automation and stronger defaults coming over time.

Patch: close known vulnerabilities faster

The need is clear in our deployment data: many Exchange Server deployments are not running the current security update, including a substantial share on unsupported versions. Closing this protection gap requires both releasing fixes faster and helping customers apply them sooner.

Today. Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed, helping customers address known vulnerabilities sooner.

Next. In Q1 calendar year 2027, we’re targeting automatic application of security updates after a fixed period following release in connected SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server environments.

Release fixes faster, then help those fixes reach servers faster.

Configure: make the safer posture easier to maintain

Security requires more than current software. Configuration and permissions can drift over time, creating gaps between the intended security posture and the environment administrators are operating. Customers need a clearer way to identify those gaps, establish recommended settings, and maintain them as environments evolve.

Today. Tenant Configuration Management can help customers assess supported SharePoint, Exchange, and Skype for Business Server environments and identify where permissions are broader than intended.

Next. In Q1 2027, we plan to introduce hardened default configurations for SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server, moving from identifying configuration risk toward establishing Microsoft-recommended security settings by default. We also plan to identify configuration drift so administrators can see when environments move away from that baseline.

Make the safer configuration easier to establish and harder to unintentionally lose.

Protect: reduce exposure when threats can’t wait for a patch

Some threats emerge before a permanent security update is available and fully deployed. During that window, customers need mitigations that can reduce exposure quickly without replacing the underlying security update.

Today. Emergency Mitigation Service can automatically apply interim mitigations for certain emerging vulnerabilities, helping reduce exposure while a permanent security update is prepared and deployed. Mitigation addresses the immediate risk; the security update addresses the underlying vulnerability.

Next. In December 2026, we plan to introduce Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 for Exchange Server and Skype for Business Server, enabling it by default and expanding the security mitigations it can apply. In January 2027, we are planning to extend Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 to cover SharePoint Server.

When threats move faster, protection needs to move faster too.

Act today, prepare for what comes next

Taken together, these investments represent an important shift: from providing customers with security guidance and tools toward building the recommended security posture into the products themselves.

Microsoft continues to recommend moving workloads to Microsoft 365 wherever possible. Start by identifying which workloads can move and which must remain on-premises. For those that remain, move to supported releases, assess exposure, apply current security updates, and enable available protections.

The Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server teams will publish additional guidance on available protections, upcoming capabilities, and actions customers can take now. We also plan to bring practitioner-focused on-premises guidance to Secure Now to help organizations assess their environment, identify critical actions, and prioritize the steps they can take.

Join us at Microsoft Ignite for Secure your on-prem estate (BRK215) to explore the initiative, upcoming investments, and steps you can take now.

Modernize where you can. Strengthen the security of what must remain.

articles.title: ​​​​What’s new in Microsoft Security: November 2026
articles.context: Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context...
articles.full_text:
Endpoint administrators need to keep elevated access accountable at scale. Security teams also need a clearer view of expert-led protection and a simpler way to deploy SQL Server protection in Azure Government. As AI agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to limit their authority and adapt protection as risk changes. This month’s Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender updates introduce capabilities across these areas, alongside new Secure AI capabilities for agent access. A recent Secure Now update in Microsoft Security Exposure Management also connects information on recent threats to focused initiatives for reducing exposure.

Here’s what’s new:

Limit agent authority to the task with Dynamic Permissions

Give agents task-scoped authority and adapt access as risk changes

As agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to manage what each agent is allowed to do. Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires. As the agent works, Dynamic Agent Risk assesses whether the agent’s authority aligns with changing behavior and context. Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond proportionately by narrowing permissions, restricting access to resources, or requiring human approval for higher-impact actions. Together, these capabilities are designed to help organizations tailor agent authority before an agent acts and adjust access as risk changes. See how security can respond when an agent steps outside its task.

Contain local AI agents with Microsoft Execution Containers

Apply least-privilege boundaries to help limit access on Windows

Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, gives organizations an operating system-enforced containment layer for AI agents, designed to limit what an agent can access. Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions, with additional isolation options for higher-risk scenarios. Organizations can tune and validate policies before enforcing them broadly, while upcoming integration with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Agent 365 is intended to extend governance and attribution across the enterprise. Discover more about this policy-driven containment for AI agents.

Scale least privilege with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Expand least-privilege scenarios with new system settings support and simpler tenant onboarding

Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management continues to expand the tasks standard users can complete without broad administrator rights. With new system settings support, standard users can change IPv4, IPv6, and DNS server values on their device’s network adapters through Endpoint Privilege Management, while administrators determine how those changes are elevated. For user-confirmed changes, administrators can require a business justification, Windows authentication, or both before the change is applied. Along with tenant onboarding updates, these improvements support organizations as they get started with and expand their use of Endpoint Privilege Management. Explore how to get started with system settings support in Endpoint Privilege Management.

Get started with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Simplify security operations with Defender Experts

See what Defender Experts are investigating in a consolidated experience

As threats move faster and security environments grow more complex, security teams need to quickly understand what matters and when to act. New Microsoft Defender Experts MDR experiences in the Microsoft Defender portal bring ongoing expert work into focus with a consolidated overview page with updated navigation and visibility into hunts. Teams can review active and completed hunts, see findings from Defender Experts, and identify items that may require follow-up. Learn more about the new Defender Experts MDR experiences.

Get around-the-clock defense with Microsoft Defender Experts MDR

Extend protection and discover local agents with Microsoft Defender

Simplify deployment and expand SQL protection

The enhanced agent for Defender for SQL Servers on machines is now generally available for resource- and subscription-level enablement in Azure Government cloud. The enhanced agent uses existing SQL infrastructure, eliminating the need to deploy the Azure Monitor Agent for this scenario. Security teams can spend less time on deployment and extend protection across their SQL Server environments. Learn more about the enhanced agent and how to get started.

Discover local AI agents and their configured MCPs on Windows and macOS

On endpoints, Microsoft Defender is extending discovery capabilities for supported local AI agents and their configured model context protocols (MCPs) across Windows and macOS. Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to help security teams understand local AI agent activity in their environment. Learn more about local agents.

Explore Microsoft Defender solutions

Improve security posture with Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Prioritize foundational security controls with Secure Now

AI-enabled attacks can take advantage of familiar weaknesses, including excessive permissions, unprotected authentication flows, and exposed systems. Secure Now now pairs information about recent threats with focused initiatives across security domains. Security teams can use that context to identify foundational controls that need attention, review the recommended actions, and prioritize work intended to reduce exposure. The update helps connect information about observed attack patterns with security improvements teams can consider in their own environments.

Learn more about Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Learn how to address agentic AI’s security challenges

From agentic inventory and observability to stopping AI runtime threats

An inventory is only the starting point for managing Al agent risk. Organizations also need to consider ownership, limits on what agents can access, how risk is reassessed as agents operate, and protections against emerging threats. “Don’t Leave AI Exposed” provides security professionals, IT administrators, and developers with actionable guidance on managing risk across the agent lifecycle. Download the guide for considerations spanning agent inventory, ownership, access, monitoring, and runtime protection.

Stay in the Loop

Security teams need a clear account of what is changing across the portfolio and where those changes can strengthen their operations. In the Loop brings together the latest Microsoft Security updates and their implications for your security strategy. Explore earlier editions and check back for the next drop.

See Microsoft Security innovations in action at Microsoft Ignite, November 17-20, 2026, in San Francisco or online.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

articles.title: How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
articles.context: Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy...
articles.full_text:
Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

Jaime Duque and Lacie Blythe are Senior Intelligence Analysts at CrowdStrike. This research was presented at Day Zero 2026.

articles.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
articles.context: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection<
articles.full_text:
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.

In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today

During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

WAF and managed rules

Bot management

Rate limiting

Caching

Transform and rewrite rules

Workers

Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins.

How it works

Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like

For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true }

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{ "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true }

The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.

The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started

Before you begin, you’ll need:

The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.

Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.

Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.

If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, configure a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges: 100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.

What comes next

Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

articles.title: Bitdefender Named a Representative Vendor in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Managed Detection and Response

articles.full_text:
For the fifth consecutive year, Bitdefender is included as a Representative Vendor in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Managed Detection and Response.

The Market Guide offers a timely opportunity to look beyond the table stakes of 24x7 alert monitoring and understand how modern MDR should leverage AI, how providers should help contain attacks, and the importance of MDR in reducing risk exposure.

As AI-enabled attacks become faster and more frequent, exposure reduction is a critical addition to detection and response.

What Do We Feel Inclusion In the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Managed Detection and Response Means?

Gartner says that more than 600 providers offer MDR services. The 30 vendors listed in the Market Guide meet the Gartner combined criteria for inclusion. Representative vendors:

Are consistently visible to Gartner clients (based on inquiries in the prior 18 months and through Gartner Peer Insights reviews from the prior 12 months)

Are variable in size and distribution to reflect the buying population

Have a clear end-user and outcome-focused offering distinct from pure technology-driven offerings

What Are Top Questions to Ask an MDR Vendor?

We believe three practical questions can help uncover whether a service is built around meaningful results.

How does the MDR vendor combine AI with human expertise to investigate threats and guide response decisions?

What actions will the MDR provider take automatically to contain an attack?

How will the MDR team help to identify weaknesses and reduce future risk?

We’ll look at these questions in detail below. They clarify whether a provider can help contain threats, reduce exposure, and support informed response decisions or if they primarily collect and escalate alerts.

MDR marketing claims can be challenging to sort out. According to Gartner: “Buyers continue to face challenges with service naming and marketing language that has often overpromised and underdelivered, adding confusion rather than clarity.”

What Is AI’s Optimal Role in MDR?

We believe AI should help security teams move faster, while people and threat intelligence guide investigations and response. According to Gartner:

“MDR must be people-focused, human-led, AI-augmented and anchored in the evidence of the successes and outcomes it delivers.”

Gartner also explains the value of this approach:

“But those services that combine automation with dynamic detection engineering and threat intelligence teams will continue to outpace an ‘automation-only’ mindset, identifying actionable countermeasures that combat the latest and most innovative threat actors.”

We believe Bitdefender MDR combines an AI-enabled SOC with round-the-clock human expertise. AI accelerates analysis and investigation, while security experts validate findings and oversee response decisions.

What Should MDR Do to Contain a Threat?

We believe an MDR provider should be ready to take agreed-upon action quickly, with clear authority and a plan to limit an attack’s spread. Alignment with your goals in this area is a key consideration for choosing the right vendor.

Gartner notes: “Assess how the MDR provider’s containment approach and incident reporting integrate with your organization. Also decide what type of actions will be performed on your behalf to align with business and compliance requirements, legal policies, and government regulations."

In our opinion, Bitdefender MDR uses pre-approved response actions to help contain threats, limit their spread, and minimize business disruption.

How Can MDR Help Reduce the Risk of an Incident?

MDR can support proactive risk and exposure reduction through threat hunting and prioritized guidance for addressing security weaknesses.

Notes Gartner: “Established MDR buyers routinely ask providers to extend their requirements beyond TDIR (threat detection and incident response) to include the proactive identification and mitigation of threat exposures.”

Bitdefender MDR leverages hundreds of millions of total covered endpoints to compile a massive amount of threat intelligence, attacker research, and threat analysis to continuously support threat hunts and update and protect customers. Our team of security experts also provides exposure insights that can help teams tackle underlying issues that might otherwise contribute to recurring risk.

Where Can You Learn More About Choosing an MDR Service?

The 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Managed Detection and Response can help security and IT leaders assess the market against their organization’s needs.

Get complimentary access to the report to inform your next MDR decision. Then explore Bitdefender MDR to learn how we believe its AI-enabled SOC and security experts can help reduce exposure, contain attacks, and extend your team’s capabilities.

articles.title: How Maven Central Builds Trust Into Dependency Delivery
articles.context: The team expects the component to be what its coordinates say it is, the metadata to help its build tool resolve the right version and related components, and the download to be...
articles.full_text:
When a development team adds a dependency, it is placing trust in more than a file.

The team expects the component to be what its coordinates say it is, the metadata to help its build tool resolve the right version and related components, and the download to be available when the build runs, wherever that build happens. Often, all of this happens automatically, without anyone having to contact the publisher or check that the service is working.

That trust is easy to overlook because the process is routine. But a public registry is part of the path between a publisher and the teams that depend on its software. How it handles publications, metadata, delivery, problems, and long-term availability affects how much confidence people can place in that path.

A registry does not establish that every component is secure or suitable for every use. Its role is to provide a dependable way to identify, publish, find, and retrieve software. That is an important part of trust in the software supply chain.

A Dependable Source Matters

For many development teams, Maven Central is the default source for Java dependencies. That default reduces friction. Developers and build tools know where to look, and publishers have a widely understood way to make release-ready components available.

Defaults also carry an expectation. Teams expect to retrieve the component they requested, with metadata that lets their tools resolve it correctly. They expect the service to be available during a local build, a CI run, or a scan. A registry that can meet those expectations consistently becomes part of the development infrastructure organisations rely on every day.

This kind of confidence is built through operational work. It begins when a publisher submits a release.

Publication Needs to Be Predictable

The registry needs to check that a submission meets the requirements for publication and can be handled consistently.

That includes:

The component's coordinates.

The structure of the files being published.

The metadata used to identify and resolve the component.

These checks support predictable publication and retrieval. They do not determine whether the software is secure, well designed, or appropriate for a particular product. Those questions depend on the component itself, how it is maintained, and the context in which it is used.

Still, predictable publication is a foundation for trust. A team needs to know that a request for a particular component and version will resolve to the files associated with that release. If information is incomplete or inconsistent, a component can be harder to discover, resolve, or use. A small problem at publication time may become a confusing failure much later, in a build pipeline far from the original publisher.

Metadata Makes Components Understandable

A registry stores files, but consumers also rely on information that describes them. Metadata helps build tools understand a component's identity, its versions, and its relationships to other components. It helps developers and automated systems find what they need.

That information has to be processed and made available alongside the files. Indexes need to be maintained so components can be searched and queried. As new versions are published, the registry needs to keep its view of the ecosystem current.

For a developer, this often feels like a simple lookup. A build tool asks for a component and gets an answer. Behind that request is work to represent, update, and serve published information in a form that clients can use.

Trust Is Becoming a Practical Requirement

This work is taking place as organisations face growing expectations to understand the software they use and how it enters their products and services.

For example:

The EU Cyber Resilience Act places due diligence responsibilities on manufacturers that integrate third-party components into products with digital elements.

NIS2 requires supply-chain security measures from entities within its scope.

DORA requires financial entities to manage ICT third-party risk as part of their wider ICT risk management.

These laws have different scopes and requirements. They do not mean that every package registry is automatically subject to the same obligations, or that using a registry makes a component compliant or secure. But they point to a broader expectation: organisations need to understand their dependencies, the sources they rely on, and the risks involved in using them.

A dependable registry can support that work by making components identifiable and reliably available, and by maintaining the information that build tools use to resolve them. It cannot make a manufacturer's risk assessment on its behalf. Confidence in a component also depends on its origin, maintenance, known vulnerabilities, and the way it is used.

Trust in the registry and trust in the component are related, but they are not the same thing. Both matter.

Availability Takes Continuing Work

Once a release is accepted, it needs to remain accessible. The registry has to manage growing volumes of files and requests, and make components available to consumers in different locations and environments.

Replication is part of that operational picture. A registry needs to make content available across the systems that serve requests while keeping files and metadata consistent. It also needs to monitor capacity and performance as usage changes. Demand is not limited to people actively writing code. Builds, test jobs, scanners, and other automated systems may all request the same component, often repeatedly.

One build fetching a dependency is unremarkable. The same request repeated across thousands of short-lived build environments becomes part of the registry's daily workload.

The service has to handle that demand while remaining dependable for everyone using it. Reliability is not something a system achieves once and then keeps automatically. It depends on continued work to operate, monitor, and improve the service.

Problems Need a Response

No shared service can assume every request will be expected or every interaction will work as intended. Registries need ways to identify and respond to abuse, unusual traffic, and operational issues. They also need people who can investigate problems and communicate with publishers and consumers when something goes wrong.

Some problems are deliberate. Many are not. A misconfigured tool, an overly aggressive automation job, or a workflow that repeatedly requests the same information can create load without anyone intending to cause harm. Understanding what is happening takes operational visibility and, sometimes, conversations with the people running the systems involved.

Support is part of that work too. A publisher may need help understanding why a release did not complete. A consumer may be trying to work out whether a failure comes from its own configuration or from the service. Clear guidance and timely responses help people resolve these issues, and help the registry team see where its processes could improve.

Dependability Has a Long Horizon

Teams build software that depends on components released years ago. They expect to resolve those dependencies as their own systems change and as new versions of build tools and operating environments arrive.

That expectation brings long-term responsibilities: retaining published files, maintaining the systems that make them discoverable, and continuing to operate the service as the ecosystem grows. A registry's role does not end when a file has been uploaded and stored.

This is easy to miss because the service often works quietly. A developer adds a dependency, a build completes, and the team carries on. The registry becomes visible when a component cannot be found, a release behaves unexpectedly, or a build fails while trying to retrieve what it needs.

By then, the work behind the service has already shaped the outcome.

Central Is Part of the Development Path

Maven Central's value comes in part from being a dependable, familiar source for Java components. Developers can build on published software, and publishers can make release-ready components available to a broad ecosystem. That convenience rests on confidence in the service and the work required to maintain it.

The more organisations rely on public registries, the more important it becomes to understand them as operational infrastructure. They receive and validate publications, process metadata, maintain indexes, serve files, respond to abuse, support users, and preserve access over time.

Maven Central should continue to make community open source broadly available. Keeping that promise means caring for the infrastructure that makes it possible, and being clear about the work on which that trust depends.

Written by Paul Horton

He is an active open source contributor who helps organisations improve software transparency and translate complex security and compliance challenges into practical solutions.

Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
articles.context: If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your...
articles.full_text:
Claude Duet (opens in new tab) is an agent, currently in research preview, that uses a cloud-based computer to do work for you. It can use all the apps and services you've chosen to connect to Claude, and it runs continuously even after you close the app. It can read your inbox, draft replies, book things, and run routines while you are away. Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day.

We built Claude Duet on three principles to guide the agent's behavior:

Your information, and what other people share in your connected apps, is handled with discretion, using a new classifier that checks messages Claude Duet drafts before they go out.

You stay in control of what it does on your behalf.

Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, sign-in tokens, or other credentials.

Claude Duet is new but the thinking behind it is not. In 2025 we published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. Since then, we have written about why no single defense is enough (opens in new tab) and why protection inside the model can’t stand alone (opens in new tab). We also build and operate the infrastructure businesses use to run agents in production through Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), and Claude Duet keeps credentials separate from the agent in the same way. It builds on this work, adding the protections that an agent acting for you needs. This post walks through what we added and what we’re still working on.

You approve important actions

An agent that acts while you’re away has to know when to stop and ask for permission before proceeding, and to do it at the right cadence. Before Claude Duet does something like sending a potentially sensitive message, paying for something, or deleting anything, it shows you the action, the destination, and the content, including every recipient. It then waits for you to approve the action.

A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code (opens in new tab) and extended for Claude Duet. It assesses whether the action matches your intent. The check runs outside the model doing the work so instructions hidden in a page cannot affect the outcome.

Some actions stay off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities, banking actions such as moving money between accounts, and accessing someone else's account. Some other steps aren’t covered by a "don't ask me again" rule, however often you have approved them, like paying or sending money, deleting an order, or creating an account. The routines that run while you are away have the same safeguards.

We spent a lot of time calibrating how often Claude Duet asks for approval. Approval fatigue is a serious issue, because too many requests teach people to tap through them, sometimes without adequate consideration. We will continue to adjust this calibration over time.

For purchases, Claude Duet pays with a one-time card from a wallet like Link from Stripe, limited to that merchant and amount. You see the item and the total, and you approve the purchase in your Link app. Your real card number isn’t shared with Claude Duet or the merchant.

Your information is handled with discretion

An agent that reads your email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where different types of information should go. If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your performance review conversations.

To address this, we built a new safety classifier that runs separately from the main model and checks whether each message Claude Duet is about to send contains potentially sensitive information. We categorize this information into two tiers:

Never share: We give the most sensitive protection to information like sign-in credentials, full card and bank account numbers, and government ID numbers. Claude Duet is instructed never to share these with anyone, even if you ask.

Needs consent to share: Claude Duet will share other private information, such as health or finances, only if you’ve explicitly approved it. Your own request counts as consent, so “send a note to my dentist about my tooth pain” generally won’t need additional approval.

If Claude Duet is blocked for either reason, it can decide to rewrite the message without the sensitive information and share with you for approval.

Claude Duet is still in research preview and these safeguards will occasionally miss something or flag a harmless message. That’s why they work alongside the approval mechanisms above, which are designed to keep you in control of what Claude Duet sends on your behalf. We expect to continue iterating on our classifier as we learn more about how people use Claude Duet.

You have visibility into tasks and connected apps

You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing in its task list, where each task has its own page, and steer it mid-task. Claude Duet keeps your conversation history and its memory so it can carry context between tasks, until you delete your history or reset it. Deleting your account wipes everything Claude Duet has stored.

The apps you have connected to Claude carry over to Claude Duet, and switching an app off in one place switches it off in both. Disconnecting an app stops new access from that moment, but what Claude Duet already learned from it stays until you reset its memory, which you can do anytime from the app’s settings. Claude Duet also uses the memory from your Claude account, so details Claude remembered from your earlier chats are visible.

Credentials and the browser are isolated from the model

Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, or the sign-in tokens for your connected apps, and it can’t save them to its memory. They only ever pass through separate machines the model can’t access, and the approvals and safety checks that govern what it does run there too.

Passwords

When a site asks for a password, you type it into a form inside the Claude app. The form encrypts it with a single-use key that exists only on our secure cloud browser machine, for that one single use. It passes the encrypted password unopened to the browser, which types it into the site. The model doesn’t see the password and can’t save or repeat it. Soon you will also be able to sign in with 1Password; Claude Duet will ask for a credential, you will approve that request in 1Password, and the credential will go to the browser without passing through the model.

An agent that signs in for you changes phishing in two ways. On one hand, Claude Duet doesn’t hold credentials for you so it can’t be phished for a password, and no hidden instruction can make it reveal a secret it doesn’t have. On the other hand, the sign-in form is itself a target, because anything that asks for a password can be imitated. So Claude Duet’s sign-in form only appears inside the app, during a sign-in you asked for. It never arrives as a link, a text message, an email, or a website other than claude.ai. If something that looks like Claude Duet asks for your password anywhere else, it’s not legitimate.

Sign-in tokens

When Claude Duet works in a connected app, it follows our Claude Managed Agents design (opens in new tab) so credentials stay out of reach of the agent’s work. Credentials that the agent uses on your behalf, such as a sign-in token for a connected service, never enter the machine where the agent works. A placeholder for the credential sits there instead and a proxy outside that machine puts in the real value only as a request is made.

The browser

Your browser in Claude Duet runs in its own dedicated virtual machine in the cloud, separate from the model and from the cloud computers the agent works on. The agent drives the browser only through a fixed set of commands: open this page, click here, type this. Whatever a site runs stays on the browser machine (opens in new tab). The site’s code and cookies don’t reach Claude Duet’s memory or your connected apps, and none of the agent’s commands can read cookies out of the browser. What does come back is the page's text and downloads, because the agent has to read them to do its job. That’s why the other checks exist, and why Claude Duet also uses the prompt-injection safeguards described in our browser-use research (opens in new tab). Files it uploads through the browser get the same sensitive-information check as its messages.

Claude Duet is also designed to identify itself as an agent. Today, requests that its web browser sends include a distinct User-Agent header, and we publish the public IP addresses it browses from, so sites can recognize it and decide how to treat it. Before launch, we also contacted several large websites and gave them the option to prevent Claude Duet from visiting their sites, and some chose to. We’ll keep refining how Claude Duet identifies itself as we learn from the research preview.

How we tested Claude Duet

Testing started well before the research preview and continues now. Our Safeguards team built evaluations from routine-shaped tasks, each in three variants: an innocent version, one with injected instructions, and one that tempts the agent to do more than it was asked. Those run alongside shadow traffic from real use.

Red teams further tested whether Claude Duet would leak information, act without approval, or follow malicious prompts. We built a threat model of the whole system, across the repositories and trust boundaries it touches. An external penetration-testing firm tested Claude Duet with access to our source code, and a follow-on engagement covering the cloud browser and the sign-in form is running now. Each new credential feature is red-teamed on an isolated rig before it ships to anyone.

Claude Duet is also in scope of Anthropic’s public bug bounty program, which rewards valid reports and offers safe harbor for good-faith research, under our responsible disclosure policy. If you find a security vulnerability, we want to hear about it: report it through Anthropic’s bug bounty program on HackerOne (opens in new tab).

Building this with you

We’re releasing Claude Duet as a research preview because we want to learn what you value in a personal agent, including the protections and controls you’d like to see next. Some of what’s described here is still changing: how often it asks for approval, how you sign in, and how well the sensitive-information checks tell what’s private from what’s harmless. Tell Claude Duet in plain words what you’d like to see or what went wrong, and it will file a report for our team.
